Image Credits: Kimberly White/Getty Images for TechCrunch
Tim Fernholz
Science Corporation’s brain tech is worth $3.5 billion after new funding
Science Corporation , the medical technology startup founded by former Neuralink president Max Hodak in 2021, raised a $400 million Series D, the company said in a blog post .
Investors in the new round valued the company at $3.5 billion, a person familiar with the deal told TechCrunch. Those backers included Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator, and PLC Neurotech.
Hodak, who talked his way into a graduate neuroscience lab as a college student and has pursued biotechnology ever since, co-founded Science to leverage new technologies to understand and interact with the brain.
Science’s first product is PRIMA, a wearable and implantable chip that helps people with age-related macular degeneration recover some vision. The device is approved in Europe and available in Germany, as well as being trialed for new conditions.
Hodak announced that the device is now being trialed for patients with another blindness-causing condition, Stargardt disease, while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.
With the funding, the company aims to bring the device to the United States through the FDA’s Humanitarian Device Exemption, which lets experimental medical technology be used to treat rare conditions. Science has convinced the FDA that advanced macular degeneration in both eyes is uncommon enough to let them seek approval to use the device on people in the U.S.
Still, the startup’s big ambition and founding purpose is connecting directly to the human brain through a bio-hybrid sensor built from a combination of cultured neurons and silicon. The company is currently designing initial human trials of the device with Yale neurosurgery professor Murat Günel, who told TechCrunch it could offer potential treatments for Parkinson’s disease, among other brain injuries and illnesses.

Corma, an Israeli-founded cybersecurity startup that builds AI models and agents for defense, has raised a $125 million Series A at a $1 billion valuation, Ynetnews reported . NEA led the round, announced on November 16, 2026, and existing investors Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures and Coatue took part. The sums check out. A $60 million seed plus a $125 million Series A equals $185 million, and the Series A makes up roughly two thirds of everything the company has raised. Several practical details remain undisclosed. The reports give no revenue figure, no named customers, no headcount we can verify and no pricing. How a $1 Billion Valuation Arrived in About Three Months
The headline on TechCrunch’s report captures the pace: a cybersecurity AI startup reaching a $1 billion valuation in about three months. Seed-stage companies rarely reprice that fast. Most security startups spend years proving that customers will pay before a late-stage investor writes a check at unicorn scale.
Two readings compete here. The optimistic one says investors saw early demand and moved quickly to secure a position in a scarce category. The skeptical one says a hot sector and a founder with a clear story can pull capital ahead of evidence. Public reporting does not let us pick between them, because no revenue, retention or deployment data has been disclosed.
The step-up in check size tells its own story. The Series A is about 2.1 times the seed, and the company has now raised $185 million in total. That is a large war chest for a business founded only a year ago. Money at that scale usually funds three things: compute, research talent and enterprise go-to-market. Which of those dominates the budget is unconfirmed, and spending breakdowns have not been disclosed.
Speed also changes the risk profile. A company valued at $1 billion after roughly a year in existence has little room to miss. Investors will expect visible customer wins within a few quarters, and the next financing round will price those wins hard. Founders in this position often find that the headline valuation helps recruiting and sales credibility, then hurts when growth normalizes.

NEA led the Series A. Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures and Coatue participated as existing investors. The mix is a mainstream Silicon Valley lineup, and it signals that the company is being priced as a platform bet rather than a niche security tool.

Estonia’s Plural raises €1bn to back Europe’s next technology giants
Plural’s team. The Tallinn- and London-based investment firm has raised €1 billion to back European technology companies in sectors including defence, energy, space and artificial intelligence. Photo: Plural.
By
Silver Tambur
· November 16, 2026 · Business · 4 minutes of reading
Share
Tweet
LinkedIn
Email
Plural, the investment firm co-founded by Estonian entrepreneurs Taavet Hinrikus and Sten Tamkivi, has raised €1 billion to back a generation of European technology companies seeking to compete on the world stage.
The firm, which operates from Tallinn and London, will invest in businesses tackling some of the continent’s most demanding technological challenges, from fusion energy and artificial intelligence infrastructure to defence and space.
The fundraising is the largest in Plural’s history and, according to figures cited by the Estonian business newspaper Äripäev, exceeds the amount raised by the entire Baltic private equity and venture capital industry last year.
It also carries a broader ambition: to help Europe build more of the companies on which its prosperity and security depend.
“For two decades, most of the world’s most valuable technology companies have been built in the US and China,” Plural said in its announcement. “Europe has been a customer rather than a creator, and that has cost us prosperity and bargaining power.”
A billion-euro commitment
The new capital is almost four times the €260 million Plural raised for its first fund in 2022 and double the €500 million raised for its second in 2024.
It will be divided roughly two to one. The larger share will finance new early-stage investments through Plural’s third fund; the remainder will go into a separate fund designed primarily to increase its stakes in leading companies already in its portfolio.
Plural’s proposition is to support founders from the outset and continue backing them as their companies grow.
“For too long, Europe has funded its best ideas in small instalments,” Carina Namih, a Plural partner, said in comments reported by Äripäev. “Founders raise a little, prove a little and then have to raise again. That is no way to build something complex.”
A field test by Estonian defence start-up Frankenburg Technologies, one of the companies backed by Plural, which has raised €1 billion in new capital. Photo: Frankenburg Technologies.
The firm’s portfolio includes Helsing in defence, Proxima Fusion in energy, The Exploration Company in space and Frankenburg Technologies, the defence company with roots in Tallinn. Plural-backed businesses have raised more than €3 billion in follow-on funding over the past year, according to the firm.
Growing ambitions
For Estonia, the fundraising offers evidence that its technology industry is developing beyond the generation of companies that established its international reputation.
Hinrikus co-founded Wise and was Skype’s first employee. Tamkivi was an early Skype executive and later co-founded Teleport. Their investment firm now backs founders attempting to build businesses in fields far removed from money transfers and internet calls.
“Several of the founders behind that success are building companies again, this time tackling much tougher challenges. Global ones,” Tamkivi told Äripäev. “Frankenburg is a good example of how a company founded in Tallinn can become an international player in the defence industry.”
Half of Plural’s team is based in Estonia, according to Hinrikus, and its funds are licensed and regulated there.
“We can see first-hand that the quality of companies coming out of Tallinn keeps improving: they are exceptionally strong technically and think globally from the outset,” he said.
Taavet Hinrikus (left) and Sten Tamkivi. Photo by Takuya Sogawa.
The scale of the fundraising is striking in its regional context. A market review by KPMG Baltics and the three Baltic countries’ private equity and venture capital associations found that their funds raised a combined €749 million in 2025. Venture capital funds accounted for €247 million of that total.
Hendrik Reimand, chairman of the Estonian Private Equity and Venture Capital Association, said Plural’s success could help other local investment firms attract international backing.
“Major investors watch one another,” he told Äripäev. “Once one has decided that Tallinn can be a base for managing capital on a European scale, others will start looking more closely at our region too.”
The trillion-dollar ambition
Plural’s partners believe attitudes towards Europe’s most technically ambitious founders are changing.
“When we started Plural, a European founder building a fusion reactor or a space exploration company was considered too risky to back,” said Khaled Helioui, another partner. “Now they are among the most sought-after founders in the world.”
The firm believes such entrepreneurs could eventually build Europe’s first trillion-dollar company. Raising capital is only one step towards that ambition; turning complex technology into commercially successful businesses remains the larger test.
Plural’s stated goal, however, is deliberately bigger than the success of any individual investment: “GDP-level impact on Europe.”

Sofinnova's Graziano Seghezzi Raises $815 Million to Fix Europe's Biotech Scale-Up Gap
Add preferred source
Sofinnova Partners has raised more than $800 million — roughly three-quarters of a billion — for a fund dedicated entirely to late-stage European biotech and medtech, a direct bet that the continent's problem is no longer invention but the capital to carry companies into commercialization. Managing partner Graziano Seghezzi, speaking at the Jefferies Global Healthcare Conference in London, argues Europe excels at company creation but remains starved of scale-up capital, and that pharma M&A — not European public markets — is the healthy exit route the industry should embrace. The evidence he offers is concrete: a $90 million Series A in Aletheia Therapeutics, a $1.5 billion sale of UK ADC-toxin developer Mirix to Novartis, and Hema now public at a valuation in the low billions. Yet the same conversation carries a counterweight. Seghezzi says Europe "cannot afford" to back fast followers against China, tells portfolio boards to treat China as a speed lever rather than a threat, and confirms Sofinnova still recommends US listings because Europe's public market lacks depth. His 2027 forecast is an up year, powered by record-level pharma M&A and a functioning, if unspectacular, IPO window.
Key Elements
Sofinnova Partners Graziano Seghezzi Aletheia Therapeutics Tea Therapeutics Mirix Surcentrix Hema Novartis Johnson & Johnson Ollin Biosciences Jefferies Global Healthcare Conference Stifel LSEG
Europe's biotech industry has spent two decades waiting for a public market deep enough to carry its best companies. Graziano Seghezzi has stopped waiting and raised three-quarters of a billion dollars to work around the gap instead.
Sofinnova Partners, where Seghezzi is managing partner, has closed a fund above $800 million dedicated entirely to late-stage European biotech and medtech — B rounds, C rounds, crossovers and companies approaching a listing. The fund was announced at Sofinnova's own growth summit in London, a couple of blocks from the Jefferies Global Healthcare Conference where Seghezzi sat down to explain it in mid-November 2026.
His thesis is narrow and specific. "We are great at technologies and company creation, but what we're still lacking a little bit is on scale-up capital," he said. The new vehicle is aimed squarely at that missing layer: European companies ambitious enough to want to bring products into commercialization rather than sell early.
A repeat of a fund that already returned exits and listings
This is not a first attempt. Sofinnova's growth team ran an earlier fund that Seghezzi says deployed roughly half a billion euros into European late-stage companies, producing a couple of exits and a couple of public listings. The new pool repeats the playbook at a larger size.
The allocation follows Sofinnova's house pattern of 70–80% biopharma and 20–30% medtech, and stays therapy-area agnostic — the target being, in Seghezzi's words, "everywhere where there is a big medical need and important solutions."

"The UK on its own is basically twice Germany, France and Italy put together," he said. "So that tells you everything about why there are bigger rounds in the UK."
Behind that scale sits a continuous flow of spin-offs and startups out of UK universities and research centers, which he credits for keeping investor interest high. The week before the interview, two Sofinnova investments together brought in about $220 million: a Series A in Aletheia Therapeutics and a Series B in Tea Therapeutics, the latter having had its Series A co-led by Sofinnova a couple of years earlier.

Munich-based Agile Robots announced on November 12, 2026 that it had closed a $500 million Series F led by SoftBank Group, with NVIDIA among the participants. The financing supports international expansion and manufacturing, putting fresh capital behind a robotics business whose research connections include Franka Robotics and a Google DeepMind partnership. Reuters confirmed the announcement .
A $500 million round for expansion and production
The round values Agile Robots at $8.5 billion and takes its total funding to $2 billion. Alongside SoftBank and NVIDIA, participants include Hitachi Group, comprising Hitachi and Hitachi Ventures, and T.Capital. The company’s November 12 announcement says the proceeds will support a larger presence in the United States, additional production capacity including in Germany, and entry into new markets.
Founder and chief executive Zhaopeng Chen described the financing as a way to accelerate expansion and bring intelligent robots into industrial production. SoftBank Investment Advisers managing partner Dennis Chang said Agile combines robotics expertise with industrial execution, adding: “We believe Physical AI will transform industries.” These are the company’s and investor’s expectations for the business.
Tech.eu’s November 12 report places the investment in an existing industrial operation: Agile’s machines assemble products, handle components, inspect equipment and move materials through factories. Its portfolio extends across robotic arms, hands, autonomous mobile robots and humanoids, together with their software and AI models.
Factory capacity and installed systems measure different things
Reuters reported that Agile opened its Fürstenfeldbruck factory, near Munich, earlier in 2026. The company says it can produce up to 10,000 legged and wheeled humanoid robots annually. That is a stated capacity ceiling, rather than a report of annual output or shipments.
Separately, Agile reports more than 20,000 robotic solutions installed worldwide. Its announcement describes deployments across automotive, consumer electronics, logistics and other industries; it does not identify that total as humanoid installations. Treating the two numbers as interchangeable would obscure the difference between the company’s established industrial business and its humanoid manufacturing ambitions.
The financing release also gives no allocation of the proceeds between the United States, German production and other markets. It therefore establishes the expansion priorities without quantifying how much additional capacity each location will receive.
A research spin-off with an academic hardware connection
Agile was founded in 2018 as a spin-off from the German Aerospace Center, according to Reuters and Tech.eu. The company reports more than 2,000 research and development specialists and over 650 patents. Its path from a public research institution into industrial automation provides a concrete technology transfer connection for universities following the investment.
There is also a direct research equipment link. Franka Robotics says it has belonged to Agile Robots since 2023. Franka describes its Research 3 system as a force-sensitive platform for robotics and AI, giving researchers low-level access to robot control and learning capabilities. Its website also says Agile’s Diana 7 now supports the Franka Control Interface, extending the ecosystem to a robot with greater reach and payload capacity.
The funding follows earlier DeepMind and NVIDIA announcements
The Series F is a financing development alongside earlier technical collaborations. On March 24, Agile announced a research partnership with Google DeepMind to combine Gemini Robotics foundation models with its hardware. The partners described an initial focus on industrial and manufacturing tasks, using deployment, data collection, training and iteration to improve their systems.
In that announcement, DeepMind robotics head Carolina Parada presented the collaboration as a step toward bringing AI into real-world applications across sectors. The research mechanism matters: operational robot data is intended to inform model development, rather than the partnership consisting only of installing a fixed model on a machine.
A separate Agile release published October 27 says NVIDIA announced plans to invest on October 19. It dates the introduction of the Agile ONE SN research humanoid at NVIDIA GTC Berlin to October 21. Those October events provide background to NVIDIA’s participation in the November round.
What this means for universities and research offices
For robotics laboratories, the connection is unusually specific: the funded group includes a research arm platform and is developing a humanoid reference platform. Agile says ONE SN uses NVIDIA’s Isaac GR00T development platform and Jetson Thor computing. Its October release also describes Diana arms supporting the Franka Control Interface, linking the company’s industrial portfolio to an interface already offered for research.
For research offices, the practical distinction is between investment, equipment access and collaboration terms. The March partnership explicitly involves operational data and model iteration. That makes data use and project outputs relevant subjects for a research collaboration agreement ; the Series F announcement itself does not supply those terms or announce university grants. This is an implication of the described research workflow, rather than a new funding opportunity for institutions.
The next stated milestone is early 2027
Agile’s October release places planned ONE SN availability in early 2027. It also describes a pilot involving Agile, Audi, Dassault Systèmes and NVIDIA at Audi’s Ingolstadt plant, where mobile humanoids pick and sequence parts. The company describes testing the workcell in a virtual twin before physical deployment.

Science's $400 million Series D funds European expansion of PRIMA while US approval remains pending.
PRIMA is CE marked in the EU but still requires FDA Humanitarian Device Exemption review before US sale.
The biohybrid neural-interface program remains research-stage with therapeutic uses still undefined.
Science Corporation announced on November 17, 2026 that it raised a $400 million Series D to expand availability of its PRIMA retinal implant in Europe, prepare for a US launch, and increase investment in its biohybrid neural-interface program.
Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator and PLC Neurotech participated, among other investors. The round brings total capital raised since Science’s founding in 2021 to more than $900 million. The company will also expand its research, manufacturing and operational infrastructure.
PRIMA’s Commercial and Regulatory Path
PRIMA is a retinal implant being studied for geographic atrophy caused by dry age-related macular degeneration. Science describes it as the first brain-computer interface CE marked in the European Union to restore form vision—the ability to read letters, numbers and words—for patients blinded by certain types of late-stage macular degeneration. It is registered for supply in the United Kingdom and is not approved or available for sale in any other country.
The implant contains 378 light-powered pixels that convert light from the system’s glasses into signals that stimulate retinal cells. The glasses combine a front-facing camera with an eye-facing projector that shines light precisely onto the implant. The design is intended to replicate the function of light-sensitive cells that have been lost.
At 12 months, 80% of patients in the PRIMA clinical study showed clinically meaningful improvement in visual acuity, and 84% reported reading letters, numbers and words at home with the system, according to Science’s product page. The reported efficacy results include the use of digital zoom and contrast.
In a July 22, 2026 announcement , Science said PRIMA had received two FDA Humanitarian Use Device designations. The program provides expedited review for devices treating rare diseases or conditions, but designation is not marketing approval: PRIMA must still be reviewed and approved through a Humanitarian Device Exemption. One designation covers blindness in both eyes caused by an advanced subset of geographic atrophy, without vision loss from other eye diseases; the other covers vision loss from Stargardt disease, a rare inherited retinal disease. The US approval process remains underway.
Biohybrid Neural-Interface Research
Science’s biohybrid architecture takes a different approach from the retinal implant: it anchors hundreds of thousands of engineered neurons to a device and uses their projections to form connections with neurons in the brain. MicroLEDs stimulate the embedded neurons, which are modified through optogenetics so they can be activated by light, while electrodes record their activity. Science says the architecture can provide orders of magnitude more bandwidth than current devices while avoiding the damage and limitations associated with inserting wires into the brain.
The company describes language and communication, motor control, and learning and reasoning after brain injuries as potential research applications for the technology.
The financing therefore supports two distinct stages of development: commercial expansion of a retinal implant still seeking US approval, and continued development of a separate neural-interface architecture whose therapeutic uses remain research objectives.

Model ML raises $250M to automate investment banking grunt work
Model ML, a London-based startup that uses AI to automate work traditionally performed by junior bankers and consultants, including building financial models, preparing pitch decks, and writing due diligence reports, has raised $250 million in Series B funding at a $1.5 billion valuation. The new round, which comes a year after its $75 million Series A round was announced, was co-led by General Atlantic and earlier backer QED Investors.
Brothers Chaz and Arnie Englander co-founded the three-year-old startup after previously co-founding two other companies, including Fat Llama, a peer-to-peer rental marketplace acquired by Swedish rival Hygglo for $41.5 million in 2022.
Model ML develops AI agents that integrate with clients’ systems, data, and tools, including Excel and PowerPoint. The startup says its agents understand the full context of deals that bankers and consultants are working on and can automatically update financial models and presentations when new developments affect their analysis.
Other startups automating the routine, repetitive tasks for investment bankers and management consultants include Hebbia and Rogo, which raised $160 million at a $2 billion valuation in April.
Anthropic and OpenAI have also built tools for financial professionals, but Model ML says it runs on open source models and that doing so allows it to operate at about 2% of the cost of frontier models while delivering faster results.

Church & Dwight Announces $225 Million Investment In BALI Hair Care Business
By Amit Chowdhry

Church & Dwight Announces $225 Million Investment In BALI Hair Care Business
Church & Dwight has agreed to acquire 45% of BALI Treatment for approximately $225 million, adding an investment in the European hair care and styling company behind BALI CURLS and BALI GENTS.
The agreement includes an option to acquire the remaining 55% beginning two years after closing.
The transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory clearance and customary conditions.
BALI reported approximately $100 million in net sales for the 12 months ended October 31, 2026.
Founded in 2022 by Hendrik Genotte, the business develops products for curly and textured hair and has expanded into men’s grooming.
Its brands have established positions in Germany and Austria, with broader European expansion underway.
Products include Hydrating Curl Cream, Curl Defining Gel, Moisturizing Conditioner and Nourishing Shampoo. The company emphasizes vegan and cruelty-free formulations and a creator-led relationship with consumers.
Church & Dwight plans to use its international capabilities to expand distribution beyond BALI’s current concentration in a limited number of European markets.
CEO Rick Dierker said the investment aligns with the company’s preference for asset-light brands with strong category positions and the potential to improve growth and gross margins.
Church & Dwight expects the investment to be accretive to cash earnings in 2027, including acquisition-related costs and interest expense.
The structure gives the company an initial minority stake and a potential path to full ownership, while BALI gains access to a larger consumer products organization.
Church & Dwight’s existing portfolio spans household and personal care brands, including ARM & HAMMER, BATISTE, WATERPIK, THERABREATH and HERO.
The investment extends its international growth strategy into a younger hair care business with established regional demand.

“BALI CARE grew from my own experience with curly hair and a desire to create products that help people embrace their natural curls. We are excited to partner with Church & Dwight, whose global capabilities and shared passion for innovation and consumer-focused solutions will help us bring our products and community to even more people around the world.”
Hendrik Genotte, Founder Of BALI Care

With distribution today concentrated in a limited number of European markets, we are poised to leverage Church & Dwight’s global capabilities to expand the brands’ reach and support their next phase of growth.
“The BALI CARE investment squarely fits into our acquisition criteria that focuses on (1) #1 or #2 brand in a category; (2) asset-light; (3) expected to be growth accretive to the Company; and (4) expected to be gross margin accretive to the Company. Our strong balance sheet will continue to provide the flexibility to add additional high-quality acquisition and investment opportunities. This capability has been a key driver of Church & Dwight’s consistently strong shareholder returns.”
Rick Dierker, CEO Of Church & Dwight

Nextchem To Acquire LNG Technologies For $220 Million
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 7:39 AM
Nextchem To Acquire LNG Technologies For $220 Million
Nextchem has signed a binding agreement to acquire liquefied natural gas process technologies from Chart Industries for $220 million in cash. The transaction will be completed through Nextchem USA and is expected to close by the end of 2026 or in early January 2027, subject to customary regulatory approvals. Chart Industries is a wholly owned subsidiary of Baker Hughes.
The acquisition will give Nextchem immediate access to established LNG liquefaction technologies, customer references, an existing backlog, a project pipeline, and a specialized engineering team.
Expanding Nextchem’s LNG Technology Portfolio
The transaction includes Integrated Pre-Cooled Single Mixed Refrigerant technology, its advanced IPSMR+ versions, early-stage IPDMR technology, and a portfolio of small-scale LNG processes.
Nextchem will also acquire more than 90 patents, trademarks, proprietary processes, and technical knowledge. Twelve professionals specializing in process engineering, business development, and commissioning are expected to join the company.
IPSMR is designed for mid-scale LNG projects with capacities ranging from approximately 0.5 million to two million tonnes per annum for each train. Its primary target range is between 1.4 million and two million tonnes.
The early-stage IPDMR platform is intended to extend Nextchem’s offering to larger projects with capacities ranging from approximately two million to more than four million tonnes per annum per train.
Small-scale LNG technologies included in the acquisition address applications below 0.5 million tonnes per annum. These include peak-shaving facilities, remote or stranded gas resources, alternative fuels, and locations without pipeline infrastructure.
Established Operations And Project Pipeline
The IPSMR platform has approximately 14 million tonnes per annum of historical operating references. Another 57 million tonnes is under construction, including a residual backlog of 30 million tonnes.
The technology has also been selected for approximately 90 million tonnes per annum of projects that have not yet reached a final investment decision.
Nextchem will gain capabilities across the project lifecycle, from feasibility studies and process design through licensing, detailed engineering, commissioning, start-up, and performance testing.
A 10-year supply agreement with Chart Industries will provide cold boxes for IPSMR projects. Cold boxes contain heat exchangers, piping, and other equipment used to cool natural gas until it becomes liquid.
The $220 million purchase price will be paid at closing and financed through dedicated credit facilities fully underwritten by BPER Banca. The price reflects a high-single-digit multiple of projected 2027 EBITDA.
Nextchem expects the acquired licensing operation to generate at least $25 million in EBITDA during 2027, with potential additional contributions from equipment sales and broader MAIRE revenue opportunities. The acquisition is expected to increase MAIRE’s EBITDA margin.
KEY QUOTES:
This acquisition represents a major step in the continued development of our technology-driven growth strategy and delivers on the ambition we set at our Capital Markets Day to expand into the LNG market. By adding proven proprietary LNG technologies, established references and highly specialised capabilities to Nextchem, we are expanding into an attractive market with a strong and flexible technology platform. At the same time, technology ownership allows us to engage with clients earlier in the project development cycle and creates further opportunities across MAIRE’s integrated model. The transaction strengthens Nextchem’s asset-light business profile while expanding the addressable market, thanks to the Group’s engineering and execution capabilities.
Alessandro Bernini, CEO of MAIRE

By Amit Chowdhry

Serena Williams And Beth Ferreira Unveil $200 Million VC Strategy Through Starfire Ventures
Serena Williams and Beth Ferreira have launched Starfire Ventures, an early-stage venture capital firm that plans to attract $200 million in capital for investments in technology-enabled and AI-native companies.
The New York-based firm will primarily invest in seed through Series A rounds, with selective participation in later-stage opportunities. Its target areas include vertical AI, business-to-business technology, and consumer businesses addressing significant but underserved needs.
Starfire’s investment strategy centers on companies that can expand access to health and wellness, education and knowledge, financial management, and consumer experiences. The firm is also interested in infrastructure that improves affordability and access, particularly in industries with more than $1 trillion of potential market value.
Within the experience economy, Starfire plans to evaluate new retail models, stadium technologies, entertainment platforms, interactive products, and other tools that increase access to or improve live and real-world experiences.
The new firm builds on an investment partnership between Williams and Ferreira that began in 2015. Their first collaboration involved a seed investment in online education company MasterClass.
They subsequently invested together in companies including pet food brand Ollie and meal delivery company Daily Harvest. Ollie was acquired by Agrolimen in 2026, while Chobani acquired Daily Harvest in 2025.
Ferreira later became an adviser to Serena Ventures when Williams launched the investment platform. She joined Serena Ventures as a general partner in 2024.
Starfire represents the next stage of the platform Williams established through Serena Ventures, which raised an inaugural $111 million fund in 2022. The new organization combines Williams and Ferreira’s more than 30 years of collective investment experience.
The pair have deployed hundreds of millions of venture capital dollars across their careers. Starfire is intended to pair that investment background with operating expertise, corporate relationships, and an international network that can help portfolio companies develop beyond their initial financing rounds.
The firm said it will evaluate not only the attractiveness of a company’s idea but also the commitment and capabilities of the founding team. This approach reflects Williams and Ferreira’s experience investing across multiple market cycles, when changes in financing conditions placed different demands on company leaders.
Starfire also plans to support founders beyond the initial capital investment. Potential assistance could include access to commercial partners, strategic guidance, hiring networks, brand development, follow-on financing relationships, and international connections.
The firm’s stated focus on critical and underserved problems suggests that it will look for businesses able to pair substantial commercial opportunities with broader access or participation. Examples could include technology that lowers costs, reaches overlooked customers, or creates new ways for people to use essential services.
Williams and Ferreira are also positioning Starfire as an enduring investment institution rather than a platform dependent entirely on its founders’ public profiles. Williams said the firm is being designed to continue beyond its current leadership and create additional opportunities for people to participate in the ownership of growing businesses.
The launch comes as AI is changing the types of companies venture investors evaluate and the ways new businesses develop products. Starfire’s inclusion of both AI-native and broadly technology-enabled companies gives it the flexibility to consider startups built entirely around AI as well as businesses using technology to modernize established industries.
Its planned stage focus will allow the firm to begin working with founders during formative periods when companies are establishing their products, hiring initial teams, developing go-to-market strategies, and identifying product-market fit.
Selective later-stage investments may give Starfire opportunities to support existing portfolio companies through subsequent rounds or participate in businesses with a clear strategic fit.
By combining the history of Serena Ventures with Ferreira and Williams’ decade-long investing relationship, Starfire enters the market as a new brand with an established record of company building, venture deployment, and founder support.
KEY QUOTES:
“Founders are looking for investors who understand their business and can be active partners as they build. Having invested through multiple market cycles, we’ve learned to look beyond a compelling idea to the conviction of the team behind it, and beyond that, we bring the operational expertise and reach to take that new generation of companies to their next stage.”
Beth Ferreira, Co-Founder and General Partner of Starfire Ventures

We’re continuing to back founders solving critical problems at their breakthrough moments, while broadening access to capital and creating opportunities for more people to participate in the ownership and growth of transformative businesses.”
Serena Williams, Co-Founder and Managing Partner of Starfire Ventures

By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 11:22 AM
Marrow Therapeutics Launches With $173 Million For Bone Marrow-Targeted Medicines
Marrow Therapeutics has launched with $173 million in combined Series A and Series B funding to develop genetic medicines for severe blood and bone marrow disorders.
The company’s $53 million Series A round was co-led by Scion Life Sciences and venBio. OrbiMed led a subsequent $120 million Series B financing.
All Series A investors participated in the Series B alongside RTW Investments, Surveyor Capital, Opaleye, NEXTBio Capital, Affinity Advisors, KKR, Spruce Street Capital, and Columbia Threadneedle Investments.
Scion Life Sciences founded Marrow Therapeutics, which is headquartered in Watertown, Massachusetts.
Developing A Bone Marrow-Targeting Platform
Marrow is developing engineered antibodies that target the transferrin receptor, also known as TfR1, in bone marrow.
The company’s Transferrin Antibody Bioconjugate platform is designed to deliver therapeutic payloads directly to bone marrow cells. Marrow plans to use this approach across multiple hematologic and bone marrow diseases.
Transferrin receptors help cells acquire iron and are present on multiple cell types. Developing medicines that engage the receptor requires controlling where therapeutic material is delivered and minimizing unintended effects in other tissues.
Marrow’s platform is intended to use engineered antibodies to reach bone marrow while avoiding off-target effects. The company is particularly focused on addressing the risk of anemia that has limited some earlier approaches involving TfR1.
Marrow believes its in vivo delivery strategy could overcome limitations associated with existing genetic medicines, including safety concerns, complex manufacturing, and restricted patient access.
These potential advantages have not yet been established in human clinical trials. The company’s programs remain in preclinical development.
Lead Program Targets Two Blood Disorders
Marrow’s lead candidate, MAR-101, is being developed for sickle cell disease and beta thalassemia.
The program is currently undergoing studies required to support an investigational new drug application.
MAR-101 is designed to decrease BCL11A and reactivate the production of fetal hemoglobin. BCL11A is a regulator involved in the transition from fetal to adult hemoglobin after birth.
Increasing fetal hemoglobin has become a validated therapeutic strategy for sickle cell disease and beta thalassemia. Fetal hemoglobin can reduce the effects of abnormal adult hemoglobin associated with these diseases.
Marrow intends to use one therapeutic approach for both conditions. The company refers to this strategy as a “pipeline in a product” because a single candidate could provide evidence supporting the delivery platform across more than one disease.
The program’s safety, durability, appropriate dose, and effectiveness will need to be evaluated through clinical studies.
Marrow is also developing additional programs for other blood and bone marrow disorders. The company has not disclosed detailed timelines or targets for those candidates.
Leadership With Transferrin Receptor Experience
Romesh Subramanian is leading Marrow as president and chief executive officer.
Tim Weeden has joined the company as chief scientific officer. His experience includes transferrin receptor biology, antibody development, and nucleic acid medicines.
John Najim is serving as chief operating officer and chief technology officer. His responsibilities include chemistry, manufacturing and controls, technical development, and business operations.
Gavriel Mullokandov is a founder and vice president of corporate development. He will support advancement of Marrow’s programs and broader platform.
The company’s leadership team has experience with earlier TfR1-based technologies that have entered clinical development. Marrow plans to apply lessons from those first-generation platforms to bone marrow delivery.
Adding Scientific And Industry Advisors
Art Levin has joined Marrow’s board of directors. Levin was the founding chief scientific officer of Avidity Biosciences and has experience developing genetic medicines.
Stuart Orkin has joined the company’s scientific advisory board. He is the David G. Nathan Distinguished Professor of Pediatrics at Harvard Medical School and an investigator at Boston Children’s Hospital through the Howard Hughes Medical Institute.
Orkin’s research has contributed to scientific understanding of fetal hemoglobin regulation and blood disorders.
The board and scientific advisory appointments give Marrow additional experience in genetic medicine, hematology, and drug development as MAR-101 moves toward a potential clinical study.
The $173 million in financing will support the lead program, development of the Transferrin Antibody Bioconjugate platform, and advancement of additional candidates.
Marrow expects to move its programs toward the clinic during the coming year, although the timing will depend on preclinical results, manufacturing work, and regulatory review.

Boyuan Capital Closes RMB 1.1 Billion ($155 Million) Industrial AI Fund
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 11:03 AM
Boyuan Capital Closes RMB 1.1 Billion ($155 Million) Industrial AI Fund
Boyuan Capital has completed the final close of its second fund with approximately RMB 1.1 billion ($155 million) in capital commitments.
Fund II will invest in industrial artificial intelligence, embodied intelligence, advanced manufacturing, and the international expansion of Chinese industrial companies.
The fund’s limited partners include national funds of funds, social-security funds, industrial groups, financial institutions, and local government-guided funds.
German outdoor power-equipment manufacturer STIHL also participated in the fund, expanding Boyuan Capital’s international industrial and corporate network.
The U.S. dollar amount is an approximate conversion and may vary with exchange rates.
Expanding Boyuan’s Industrial Investment Strategy
Boyuan is Bosch Group’s only market-oriented investment platform. The firm combines financial investment with access to Bosch’s engineering knowledge, value chain, industrial applications, customers, and international operations.
Fund II builds on Boyuan’s earlier investment activity across automotive technology, new energy, and intelligent manufacturing.
The new vehicle will focus more directly on applying AI within industrial environments. Boyuan is targeting technologies that can move beyond laboratory demonstrations and operate at commercial scale in manufacturing, robotics, automotive, energy, and other physical industries.
The firm plans to evaluate whether a company’s technology can solve identifiable industrial problems, be integrated into existing production environments, and generate products or services that can be delivered consistently at scale.
Boyuan will also examine whether portfolio companies can use China’s engineering and manufacturing capabilities to compete in international markets.
Creating Companies Through Industrial Partnerships
Fund II’s strategy includes creating new businesses through carve-outs and joint incubation projects connected to Bosch and other industrial partners.
A carve-out can transform a technology, operating unit, or internal project into an independent company. Joint incubation allows Boyuan to combine the technical capabilities of an established industrial group with a new management team and outside capital.
This approach is intended to give young companies access to real industrial environments earlier in their development. It may also help them validate products with potential customers before investing in broader commercialization.
Boyuan plans to identify technologies within Bosch’s value chain that could become independent businesses. The firm will also pursue joint ventures with other manufacturers and technology partners.
Seven Initial Portfolio Companies
Fund II has already invested in seven companies.
The portfolio includes Bowintec, which was jointly incubated by Boyuan and Galbot, and Weifu Smart Sensing, a company created with Weifu High-Tech and Bosch.
Boyuan has also invested in robotics companies Linkhou Robotics and Inspire Robots. These investments reflect the fund’s focus on embodied intelligence, where AI systems interact with physical environments through robots, sensors, and automated equipment.
Another portfolio company, X-Motors, is pursuing international expansion beginning in Indonesia. Its strategy illustrates Boyuan’s effort to help Chinese advanced manufacturing companies establish operations and customer relationships outside their domestic market.
The fund intends to continue investing across industrial AI, robotics, sensing technology, automotive systems, and other areas where software, hardware, and manufacturing capabilities intersect.
Supporting Commercialization And Global Expansion
Boyuan plans to provide more than financial capital through its OpenBosch and Bo-ignition programs.
These initiatives connect portfolio companies with engineering expertise, industrial customers, real-world applications, and international networks.
The firm can help companies evaluate whether a technology works within an operating factory, vehicle, energy system, or other industrial setting. It can also support product validation, customer introductions, and the development of commercial operations.
For companies seeking international growth, Boyuan intends to provide connections to overseas industrial partners and markets. This assistance could include identifying local customers, adapting products to regulatory requirements, and establishing business operations outside China.
The participation of STIHL adds another international industrial organization to the fund’s network. Boyuan expects relationships with global manufacturers to support technical collaboration and potential commercialization opportunities for its portfolio companies.
Fund II’s strategy reflects the growing effort to apply generative AI, machine learning, robotics, and intelligent sensing to physical industries. Boyuan’s investment approach will emphasize whether these technologies can produce measurable operational and commercial results.
KEY QUOTES:

November 16, 2026

Round led by Highland Europe, alongside Morgan Stanley Investment Management’s 1GT and Axon Partners Group, and with participation from existing and new investors.
BARCELONA, SPAIN – November 16, 2026 – ( Motor Sports NewsWire ) – Stark Future, the Barcelona company behind the world’s best-selling enduro motorcycle, today announced the close of a financing round with a total transaction value in excess of €150 million, the largest investment ever made in a European electric motorcycle company. The round values Stark Future at €1.2 billion pre-money, making it Europe’s first electric motorcycle company valued above €1 billion. The round was led by Highland Europe, alongside Morgan Stanley Investment Management’s 1GT climate private equity strategy and Spain-based international investment firm Axon Partners Group, with participation from existing shareholders and friends and family. The round was oversubscribed and exceeded the initial target, prompting the Company to keep the door open for a second closing to accommodate additional strategic partners, including Lombard Odier among others.
Founded in 2020 on an uncompromising belief that electric motorcycles should not just be the green alternative, but the better machine, Stark Future builds bikes designed to beat the best combustion competitors in every category they enter. Today, the VARG platform, spanning motocross, enduro and supermoto, is designed, engineered and built in-house at the Company’s 20,000 m² facility on the outskirts of Barcelona. The new capital will fund global expansion and the development of new electric platforms.
In just three years of sales, Stark has gone from challenger to category leader. The VARG is now the best-selling enduro motorcycle on the planet, outselling every combustion competitor. Within its first year, Stark took around 50% of the enduro market in Germany and the top spot in France and Italy, while the United States has grown to be its largest market by volume. From a standing start, Stark has taken around 5% of the €3 billion global off-road motorcycle market from combustion in three years. The new capital is aimed at repeating that, and more, by entering new motorcycle categories, in a much larger €90 billion addressable motorcycle market. Few hardware companies grow this fast. Fewer do it profitably.
Anton Wass, Founder and CEO of Stark Future, says: “Six years ago, Stark was an unwavering belief that electric could be the better machine, not the compromise. Today it’s the largest investment ever made in a European electric motorcycle company. We turned the industry on its head once with the VARG, taking 5% of a €3 billion market from combustion in three years. This gives us the resources to do it again, and more, in a €90 billion market. While others in this industry have run out of road, we’ve grown, turned profitable, and brought Highland Europe and world-renowned institutional investors on board, and we have kept the door open in the second closing for a few more who share the same ambition. None of it would have happened without the riders who chose a VARG before the world’s biggest investors did, and the dealers who put it on their floors. Thank you for making this dream real. We’re not here to take part in the future of motorcycling. We’re here to lead it.”
Tony Zappalà, Partner at Highland Europe, added: “Since selling its first bike just three years ago, Stark Future has become the go-to name in performance off-road motorcycling. It has built that traction in the most technical and unforgiving segment of the market. Once we met with Anton and the team, we caught the fever of the company’s guiding principle: to build the best bike with no compromises. Motorbikes are the last major vehicle category to meaningfully undergo electrification. Many have tried, but no one has matched Stark’s success. We believe it will be the company that leads the transition with best-in-class performance.”
Vikram Raju, Head of Climate Private Equity Investing at Morgan Stanley Investment Management and 1GT, said: “The most compelling climate solutions are often those that do not ask their customers to compromise. Stark Future is a powerful example of that, combining a relentless focus on engineering excellence with electric motorcycles built to compete on performance first. At 1GT, we back ambitious founders and teams whose products and solutions have the potential to create meaningful real-world impact and advance the transition to a lower-carbon economy. We are excited to support the company’s next phase of growth and look forward to bringing the resources and global capabilities of Morgan Stanley to the partnership as Stark continues to scale internationally.”
Alfonso de León, Managing Partner at Axon Partners Group , said: “Stark is the rare technology and performance company that grows like a tech business and earns like an industrial one. As a Spanish-based investment firm, Axon is proud to invest alongside Highland, 1GT, and a group of world-class investors to support a Spanish company leading a global category. This is just the beginning of what Stark will become.”
Stifel served as the lead financial adviser to Stark Future for this transaction. This investment brings long-term backing from major institutional investors, including Highland Europe, whose portfolio features category-leading companies such as Wolt, GetYourGuide, Huel, and Zwift, alongside Morgan Stanley Investment Management’s 1GT strategy, Axon Partners Group and Lombard Odier. Together, they give Stark Future the capital and reach to turn its leadership in electric off-road into a global force in motorcycling.

News provided by

New energy-efficient, emissions-free process for metallization to scale from the company's pilot line near MIT to 1,000 metric tons per year of commercial production in 2027
CAMBRIDGE, Mass. , Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- General Flash, which has developed a fundamentally new way to make critical metals, today announced it has raised $128 million in equity capital across its Seed and Series A rounds to scale domestic production of metals essential to national security and American manufacturing. Investors include Lux Capital, Construct Capital, Overmatch Ventures, GreatPoint Ventures, Pillar VC, Lowercarbon Capital, Ensemble VC, Ravelin and leading angel investors.
Critical metals and minerals like tungsten, titanium, zirconium, tantalum and rare earths go into semiconductors, defense, aerospace and advanced manufacturing. In the 20th century, the United States developed most of the techniques used to make these materials but allowed production to move overseas, and today it depends heavily on foreign supply. Although these minerals are mined around the world, China accounts for more than 80% of refining capacity for many of them. Starting January 1, 2027, Department of War rules will bar Chinese supply for many of these critical materials from U.S. defense supply chains.
General Flash's process converts metal oxides directly into high-purity, semiconductor-grade metal, with no emissions. It is faster and lower cost than conventional refining and gives the U.S. a way to build cost-effective refining capacity at home instead of relying on foreign supply. The company's Solid-State Flash Electrolysis (SSFE) process is metal-agnostic and can be used to refine materials like tungsten, tantalum, titanium, hafnium, zirconium, germanium, yttrium, niobium, molybdenum, and rare earth elements.
The funding will support commercial-scale production by summer 2027, in what will be one of the largest and most advanced critical materials production plants in the world.
"Critical metals are foundational to every advanced industry," said Ric Fulop, Co-Founder and CEO of General Flash and member of the visiting committee of the MIT Department of Materials Science and Engineering and research scientist at the MIT Center for Bits and Atoms. "We started General Flash because we believe there's a better, cleaner and more efficient way to make these materials. We've already demonstrated it at our multi-ton pilot facility near MIT, and this funding fully finances production of our first large plant in the U.S."
"Every advanced industry runs on critical metals, and the way we make them has barely changed in decades," said Peter Hebert, Co-Founder and Partner at Lux Capital. "General Flash has a genuinely new process, proven at pilot scale, and a founder who has built and scaled a manufacturing company before. We believe it can become one of the most important American industrial companies of the next decade."
"Foundational industries like metals production rarely sprout new companies, but that is exactly what is needed today as demand for onshore critical metals suppliers has skyrocketed," said Dayna Grayson, Co-Founder and Managing Partner at Construct Capital. "General Flash is showing that critical metals can be made in America with a cleaner, more efficient process, and that the next generation of heavy industry can be built here."
"America's defense supply chain depends on metals that are refined almost entirely overseas, and new Department of War rules make that dependence impossible to ignore. General Flash gives the U.S. a way to make these materials at home, at scale, and that matters for national security," said Jordan Blashek, General Partner at Overmatch Ventures.
"General Flash is solving one of the most pressing challenges facing the U.S.: secure access to critical materials," said Andrew Perlman, Founding Managing Partner at GreatPoint Ventures. "Its technology can strengthen the American supply chain while bringing down costs, and its founders have exactly the kind of big vision we're proud to back."
About General Flash
General Flash makes critical metals using a new solid-state process that converts metal oxides directly into metal, with no emissions. Based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, the company operates a 20-metric-ton-per-year pilot facility near MIT and is scaling to commercial production for defense and commercial customers. Its process is being developed for tungsten, tantalum, titanium, hafnium, zirconium, germanium, yttrium, niobium, molybdenum and rare earth elements. Learn more at generalflash.com .

Defensive-cybersecurity company Corma announced on November 16, 2026 that it had raised a $125 million Series A at a $1 billion valuation. NEA led the round, with continued participation from Sequoia Capital , Khosla Ventures and Coatue, bringing Corma’s total funding to $185 million.
Corma said the new capital would accelerate scaling of its foundation models, expand compute capacity and support selective hiring. The Series A follows its emergence from stealth on August 10, 2026 with $60 million in seed funding.
The company characterized demand from the world’s largest organizations as overwhelming and identified securing enough compute for that demand and its waitlist as one of its central challenges. Corma’s ability to expand access therefore depends on obtaining additional infrastructure as well as advancing its models.
How the Corma Workforce Operates
The company deploys those models through the Corma Workforce , a system designed to work autonomously alongside human security teams. It operates within customers’ existing security and IT stacks, including identity, cloud, endpoint, security information and event management, and firewall or intrusion-detection tools. Its work spans investigations, connecting evidence and taking action across those systems.
Employees can assign tasks through Slack or Teams, ask questions, review findings and approve actions. The design adds AI-led execution to a customer’s current operating environment while keeping human review in the workflow.
Corma reports live deployments across healthcare, finance, energy, critical infrastructure and retail, with 99% of security tasks completed autonomously and successfully, 100 times faster end-to-end completion and 95% lower cost per completed task.
One anonymized Fortune 1000 services-company CISO quoted on the product page said end-to-end response time fell 94% in a comparison with the customer’s former service provider, which the customer subsequently replaced with Corma.
Why Corma Uses Defense-Specific Models
Corma’s launch statement argues that improvements in coding and software reasoning map more directly to offensive security than to the broader defensive workload. Vulnerability research and exploit development are code-reasoning problems against bounded targets; defense instead requires continuous analysis of audit logs, events, configurations and network flows. It also involves connecting weak signals across systems and long periods while making thousands of accurate, consistent decisions each day under changing conditions.
That distinction is the basis for Corma’s focus on domain-specific foundation models. Its stated development program includes rethinking model architecture, extending context to detect faint anomaly signals, adversarial self-play and continuous learning that can establish baselines over months and years.
CEO Alon Pluda and the Corma team said the next generation of its foundation models would be shared soon, without giving a release date. The financing supports that next phase of model development and selective hiring, but the immediate scaling constraint is compute: broader deployments require enough additional capacity to serve current demand and organizations on the waitlist.

Israeli AI language model cybersecurity company Corma , today announced the completion of a $125 million Series A financing round, at a $1 billion valuation, led by NEA, alongside existing investors Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures. The company has now raised $185 million, having emerged from stealth just three months ago with a $60 million seed round led by Sequoia.
CEO Alon Pluda founded the company last year, after leaving Miggo Security, which he cofounded, following a dispute with his cofounders. Pluda is a graduate of the IDF Intelligence Corps’ prestigious Psagot program. He completed his service in 2022, following several years as a career officer in various technical roles at the core of Unit 8200’s technological operations. He founded Corma, which has 20 employees in Tel Aviv and San Francisco, with the aim of more effectively addressing AI-driven cyberattacks. The company achieves this by developing language models from scratch, rather than relying on existing models such as those from Anthropic, OpenAI, and DeepSeek.
Pluda explains, "General-purpose language models are effective for tasks like software development or research and they are also excellent at identifying bugs and cyber vulnerabilities, which is precisely why hackers and attackers use them so efficiently. However, they are weak when it comes to defense. Defense requires a different kind of expertise: the ability to find a 'needle in a haystack' within the complex landscape of enterprise data systems, specifically regarding code and software maintenance, such as telemetry, logs, and events."
In Pluda’s view, this is why the language models currently on the market are highly advanced in their capacity to facilitate powerful cyberattacks, yet remain insufficiently developed for the purpose of defending organizations. Fluda explains that Corma addresses this gap by developing its own language model, which is focused entirely on a single task: perimeter defense for organizations. The company also develops AI agents that are integrated into client organizations, working alongside existing cybersecurity teams.
Pluda adds, "We don’t just provide CISOs with a dashboard or software to manage. We provide AI agents that empower them, enabling them to perform their jobs orders of magnitude better."
The company trains its models with the goal of achieving "superintelligence" for defensive cybersecurity - a capability that will allow security teams to operate at the speed and scale required to counter the advancement of AI-driven cyberattacks.
The company’s annual recurring revenue (ARR) is estimated to be in the tens of millions of dollars, and its client base includes companies from the Fortune 100 and Fortune 500 lists.
"Since its initial unveiling in August, demand for the company’s models has surged among organizations ranked in the Fortune 100, Fortune 500, and Fortune Global 500. To meet this demand, the company has increased its server capacity 24-fold," the company stated.
Corma works with large organizations, including companies in the healthcare, financial services, energy and critical infrastructure, retail, and telecommunications sectors. These organizations are increasingly delegating their security tasks to Corma’s autonomous workforce, which operates using a foundational model developed by the company.

General Dynamics Business Units Receive $117.6 Million In Navy Contract Actions
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 10:53 AM
General Dynamics Business Units Receive $117.6 Million In Navy Contract Actions
General Dynamics business units received three Navy contract actions with a combined announced value of approximately $117.6 million for enterprise IT services, Virginia-class submarine materials, and undersea research.
The combined figure consists of a $56 million ceiling increase for General Dynamics Information Technology, a $41.6 million undefinitized contract action for General Dynamics Electric Boat, and a $20 million research contract for General Dynamics Applied Physical Sciences. The amounts have different funding and contract structures and should not be interpreted as $117.6 million in guaranteed or immediately obligated revenue.
General Dynamics Information Technology received a modification increasing the ceiling of indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract N0003925D7800 by $56 million, from $98.5 million to $154.5 million. The additional ordering capacity will support the Navy’s effort to consolidate legacy help desks into the Navy Enterprise Service Desk by October 1, 2027.
The consolidation supports the Secretary of the Navy’s Operation Cattle Drive mandate. Work will continue in Bossier City and New Orleans, Louisiana, with each location accounting for 50% of performance.
The GDIT contract is in its second performance year under an option period running from August 2026 through August 2027. One optional year remains and could extend performance through August 2028. The government did not report an immediate obligation associated with the ceiling increase, so the $56 million represents additional potential ordering authority rather than a funded task order.
The production contract followed GDIT’s successful completion of an Other Transaction Authority prototype effort that began in 2019. Portfolio Acquisition Executive Mission Systems in San Diego is the contracting activity.
General Dynamics Electric Boat received a $41.6 million undefinitized action under previously awarded contract N00024-24-C-2124. The action supports the procurement of long-lead materials for Virginia-class submarines.
Electric Boat will perform the reported work in Franklin, Massachusetts, with completion expected in June 2031. The Navy will obligate approximately $18.9 million in fiscal 2025 other procurement funding at award. Those funds will expire at the end of the current fiscal year.
Because the action is undefinitized, the Navy and Electric Boat will finalize certain pricing or contractual terms later. Long-lead procurement enables specialized materials and components to enter production early enough to protect submarine construction schedules. The Supervisor of Shipbuilding, Conversion and Repair in Groton, Connecticut, is the contracting activity.
General Dynamics Applied Physical Sciences received a $20 million cost-plus-fixed-fee completion contract for Advancements in Undersea Dominance and Naval Engineering.
The Groton, Connecticut-based business will conduct studies and develop naval technologies using first-principles analysis and physics-based modeling and simulation. Work will be performed in Groton through September 2031.
The Navy will obligate $5.1 million in fiscal 2026 research, development, test, and evaluation funding at award. Those funds will not expire at the end of the current fiscal year.
The five-year research contract has no options and was competitively procured through the Office of Naval Research’s long-range broad agency announcement for Navy and Marine Corps science and technology.
Across the three actions, the Navy reported approximately $24 million in funding obligated at award. This total comprises Electric Boat’s $18.9 million obligation and Applied Physical Sciences’ $5.1 million obligation. No immediate obligation was reported for GDIT’s $56 million ceiling increase.

Noeri, an enterprise AI startup co-founded by two Stanford University artificial intelligence professors, has officially unveiled itself and announced it has raised $110 million. The round was led by Menlo Ventures, with participation from Madrona Venture Group, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA, while Cisco's investment arm, Nvidia and Snowflake joined as strategic investors. The company's valuation was not disclosed.
Noeri was founded only about five months ago and is headquartered in Palo Alto, California. Its co-founders are Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin. Choi was previously a distinguished scientist at Nvidia and received a MacArthur Fellowship in 2022; Guestrin is one of the co-developers of the open-source machine learning tool XGBoost, and his earlier machine learning company Turi was acquired by Apple in 2016, after which he led Apple's core machine learning and AI teams. The company's name evokes the idea of "multiple intelligences," and it is currently hiring research and engineering talent in Palo Alto and Zurich.
The company's starting point came from cost considerations at a Stanford microbiology and immunology research team. According to Choi, who spoke to Bloomberg , the team considered GPT-5 too expensive, so it trained a small AI to schedule work by older models such as GPT-4. The combination of "a small model directing older models" ended up outperforming GPT-5 on specific tasks.
Building on that discovery, Noeri is focused on so-called "self-improving" AI systems: the tool examines a company's existing AI models, software development tools and other software, identifies areas for adjustment and proposes modifications—retraining underlying models when necessary. All changes must pass human review before going live, allowing the system to continuously learn from a company's own data and workflows and gradually form specialized models that are cheaper and better tailored to specific business needs, while companies retain the models and processes they have built themselves.
Noeri is not alone on this path. Japan's Sakana AI launched Fugu in June this year, which likewise uses specially trained models to direct other AIs in completing complex tasks, and it is investing in AI self-improvement research. Noeri's difference lies in its explicit focus on enterprise scenarios and its emphasis on absorbing internal corporate data and practical experience over the long term.
The round's backers span both venture capital and industry strategic investors. The participation of Nvidia, Cisco and Snowflake reflects growing interest among large technology companies in "replacing a single flagship model with low-cost model combinations." For enterprise users, if self-improving systems can genuinely lower inference costs and improve accuracy on specific tasks, they would offer an alternative to an AI spending structure currently heavily dependent on a handful of large models. Still, because such systems involve model retraining and workflow changes, the barriers to adoption and governance costs remain key things to watch.

PHOENIX , Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Trinity Capital Inc. (NYSE: TRIN ), a leading alternative asset manager, today announced the commitment of $100 million in debt financing to Phononic, a North Carolina-based company developing solid-state cooling solutions for AI data centers. The financing will support accelerated growth and manufacturing capacity expansion to meet increasing customer demand.
Phononic's proprietary Thermal Control Systems™ provide software-defined cooling for AI infrastructure by combining high-performance thermoelectric devices with intelligent controls. Compact, solid-state devices and an integrated software control layer deliver precision cooling at the point of need for critical components, including GPUs, high-bandwidth memory, networking silicon, and the optical transceivers that connect them. Phononic's Thermal Fabric™ software layer monitors conditions throughout the data center and dynamically adjusts thermal control in real time as AI workloads change. Together, these solutions are designed to unlock greater AI infrastructure performance, optimize compute and facility capacity, and reduce energy and water consumption.
"As AI hardware continues to evolve, we believe precise, real-time cooling at the chip level is becoming increasingly important," said Phil Gager, Senior Managing Director of Tech Lending at Trinity Capital. "Phononic has built the thermoelectric technology and software to address that need, and we're pleased to back their team as demand for their solutions continues to build."
Phononic enters its next phase of growth as a profitable company backed by leading venture and growth-equity investors. With demand accelerating across AI infrastructure, the company is expanding manufacturing capacity to meet growing customer requirements and scale delivery of its intelligent thermal control solutions.
"AI infrastructure is advancing at an unprecedented pace, and cooling has become a critical bottleneck to growth, limiting both facility capacity and compute and optical performance. Our customers are demanding disruptive thermal control solutions that can overcome these limitations at scale," said Dr. Tony Atti, CEO and Founder of Phononic. "Our partnership with Trinity Capital enables us to accelerate manufacturing capacity expansion to meet that demand and support the next wave of growth across AI infrastructure."

Deployed across major U.S. hyperscalers, Phononic's solutions deliver precision thermal control at the source for optical connectivity, GPUs, high-bandwidth memory, and other critical AI components. Remedy Robotics, a San Francisco medtech treating stroke patients remotely, and cofounded by Perth-born doctor David Bell, has raised US$62 million (A$92m) in a Series B, backed by a range of Australian venture funds.
US venture firm DCVC led the round, with existing backers Blackbird, Tony Fadell’s Build Collective, Divergent Capital and KdT Ventures chipping in alongside the the University of California’s investment office, Skip Capital and super fund Hostplus as new investors.

Bell spent eight years in medicine, including cardiac surgery and air retrieval, before studying at Stanford, where he met his cofounder and CTO Jake Sganga. “This funding will allow our world-leading hardware, software, and machine learning teams to progress the N1 system towards clinical trials and potential FDA approval, while also developing additional features including full autonomy,” Sganga said.

Project Omega Raises $80 Million To Develop Nuclear Fuel Recycling Infrastructure
By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 11:10 PM
Project Omega Raises $80 Million To Develop Nuclear Fuel Recycling Infrastructure
Project Omega has raised $80 million in Series A financing to develop nuclear fuel recycling infrastructure and long-duration power products. B Capital led the round, with participation from noa VC, 645 Ventures, and other investors focused on nuclear technology and national security. Existing investors Starship Ventures, Mantis Ventures, Decisive Point, Virta Ventures, Pace Ventures, Essential Capital, and Washington Harbour Partners also participated.
B Capital General Partner Jeff Johnson will join Project Omega’s board of directors.
The company is developing a non-aqueous pyroprocessing platform intended to recover useful materials from spent nuclear fuel. Its technology targets isotopes that can be used in long-duration power systems, reactor feedstock, and commercial, scientific, and medical applications.
Project Omega said the process does not separate pure plutonium and could reduce nuclear-waste volume by up to 90%.
Its initial products include radiovoltaic systems that convert the natural decay of radioisotopes directly into electricity. Potential applications include sensors, autonomous systems, communications infrastructure, spacecraft, undersea platforms, and equipment deployed in areas where battery replacement is difficult.
Project Omega has worked with Idaho National Laboratory through the ARPA-E CURIE program and demonstrated stable electrical current from strontium-90 at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. It has also developed radioisotope power systems through DARPA’s Rads to Watts program.
The financing will support a pilot facility for isotope recovery and feedstock production, construction of a nuclear fuel recycling facility, and further development and manufacturing of the company’s X Series expeditionary power systems.
Project Omega has offices in Newport, Rhode Island, and Hailey, Idaho, along with a laboratory in Fall River, Massachusetts.
KEY QUOTES:
America’s growing demand for reliable power is colliding with a nuclear fuel cycle that remains dependent on foreign supply and leaves enormous value stranded in used fuel. Project Omega’s technology has the potential to create multiple revenue streams from a largely untapped domestic resource, spanning long-duration power, reactor feedstock and strategic isotopes. We’re excited to support Staff Sheehan and his highly experienced team as they scale this platform and unlock economic potential across the nuclear value chain.
Jeff Johnson, General Partner and Global Head of Energy at B Capital
The country’s nuclear renaissance will not happen without the fuel. We have a domestic source for this, nearly 100,000 metric tons of used nuclear fuel, which is one of America’s largest untapped energy resources. We are building a vertically integrated strategy around an abundant domestic feedstock, with a non-aqueous recycling process that recovers useful isotopes, and products with clear strategic demand. That combination creates the potential for an entirely new nuclear innovation economy.
Stafford Sheehan, Founder and CEO of Project Omega
Project Omega has progressed well beyond a compelling scientific idea. The company is building the fuel-cycle infrastructure needed to support America’s growing nuclear industrial base and help power the country’s next era of innovation.
Howard Morgan, Co-Founder, Chair and General Partner at B Capital

China ‘s robotics companies continue drawing fresh investment in humanoids , robot chips and training models, led by UniX AI’s 500 million yuan (about $75 million) Pre-A round. Other developments include a 400-unit UBTech humanoid order, Hesai’s third-quarter results and Huawei Cloud’s release of an open-source robot world model .
UniX AI
UniX AI , which makes wheeled humanoid robots for security, hotels and retail, has raised 500 million yuan (about $75 million) in a Pre-A round, Science and Technology Daily reported , citing the Suzhou company. Existing investors Xienuo and Yonghua added to their stakes. New backers include Greenland Group, a customer that joined as a strategic investor, along with Keli Sensing, HUST Ventures and others. UniX said it ships more than 100 robots a month, with peak monthly output above 300, and has batch orders from property groups, Certis and Inspur. Proceeds will fund algorithm research, product updates and wider use in property management, hotels and retail.

TensorWorld, which was founded in July and is building physics-based foundation models that predict how objects move and interact, has raised more than $100 million across an angel round and an angel-plus round, according to a Starlink Capital post published by 36Kr . Nigerian businessman, Mr Tony Elumelu, has acquired an additional $70 million stake in Seplat Energy Plc through his energy investment firm, Heirs Energies Limited, increasing its shareholding in the energy firm to 22.05 per cent.
