The company’s chief executive, Mr Osa Igiehon, said in an interview last month that increasing its holding in Seplat aligns with its growth strategy, which also includes raising oil production to 100,000 barrels per day by the end of the decade.
Meanwhile, Mr Elumelu is expected to assume the position of Chairman of Seplat on January 1, 2027, succeeding Mr Udoma Udo Udoma, who is due to retire from the organisation’s board on December 31, 2026.

LanceDB raised $57.5 million to expand a lakehouse that curates and serves AI training data.
The company reports more than tenfold year-over-year revenue growth since its Series A in June 2025.
LanceDB aims to unify training data, experiments and rollouts so teams stop hand-managing pipelines.
LanceDB announced on November 17, 2026 that it raised $57.5 million in Series B funding to expand its multimodal lakehouse, a platform for organizing and delivering AI training data. The round brings the company’s total funding to $98.5 million.
Bessemer Venture Partners and Innovation Endeavors led the round, with participation from Theory Ventures, Dimension, Swift Ventures, CRV and Y Combinator. LanceDB plans to put the capital toward a broader role across model development, including training-data management, feature engineering, experiment execution and data loading.
Adoption and Technical Scale
LanceDB says researchers can lose weeks or months obtaining and curating training data even though frontier AI advances are measured in days and weeks. Its multimodal lakehouse is intended to close that gap by combining curation, search and retrieval, feature engineering and training for work on frontier models, world models, physical AI and enterprise applications.
The company reports more than tenfold year-over-year revenue growth since its Series A in June 2025. Its open-source library has been downloaded more than 120 million times, representing sixfold growth in total downloads from the same point a year earlier. Customers include Netflix, Microsoft AI, Runway , Luma AI and Midjourney.
The platform is designed to hold multimodal data such as videos, images and sensor data while supporting large-scale retrieval and training. LanceDB says the platform supports more than 130,000 requests per second with latency below 210 milliseconds for 95% of requests, individual tables containing hundreds of petabytes of data or more than 40 billion vectors, and training across 8,000 GPUs in parallel.
Enterprise additions address updates to those tables while they are in use. A durable, memory-accelerated write path handles real-time ingest, distributed indexing scales across large datasets, and managed compaction continuously optimizes tables in the background. LanceDB says managed compaction supports up to 100 billion multimodal rows while multiple researchers concurrently read, write and query the same table.
Customers Describe Changing Training Datasets
Runway CTO Kamil Sindi described how one training example evolves: “A training example at Runway doesn’t stay still. It starts as a video and a prompt, then we add embeddings, resolution and duration metadata, whatever the next experiment needs.” Runway began using the Lance data format in 2024 and later became a LanceDB Enterprise customer. The company now uses Lance and LanceDB Enterprise together so researchers can work through large, changing datasets more quickly.
NVIDIA Cosmos, an open-source user and partner, provides another deployment example. Technical lead Max Li said the team curated roughly one million hours of video with Lance for Cosmos 3, is moving toward training directly from the format, and finds its object-storage-native architecture useful for streaming, filtering and inspecting large datasets as they are revised while supplying data to large GPU clusters.
Microsoft AI data-platform head Suqiang (Jack) Song said his organization uses LanceDB as its training-data layer for billions of rows spanning images and code, with distributed inference jobs reading Lance directly on thousands of nodes; operating within Microsoft’s own tenant and security policy was non-negotiable for production.
Series B Roadmap
LanceDB intends to bring training data, context, logs and rollouts into one system at petabyte scale. Research teams would also be able to run large numbers of AI-agent experiments in parallel without contaminating shared datasets. The work is aimed at the full model-improvement cycle, reducing the manual pipeline oversight and data-loading problems that can slow research.
LanceDB also plans to deepen its feature-engineering tools. A team would define a transformation once, after which the platform would apply it throughout the dataset, backfill existing rows and process new data as it arrives. Further work targets more of the preparation done before training, plus better data loading and caching during training runs.
The Series B pushes LanceDB beyond retrieval into the continuing work of changing datasets, conducting experiments and supplying training jobs. Its next phase will test whether one platform can accommodate both frontier-scale data volumes and the constant, experiment-by-experiment changes described by customers such as Runway.

candidates.title: AI-Native CRM Dreamteam Raises $53 Million in Seed and Series A Funding
candidates.snippet: AI-Native CRM Dreamteam Raises $53 Million in Seed and Series A Funding Wowtale
candidates.text:
For more than two decades, CRMs such as Salesforce and HubSpot have depended on salespeople remembering to type in what happened on a call. When they forget, customer context disappears and the pipeline fills with stale data. Dreamteam , an AI-native CRM built on the opposite premise, said it raised $53 million from Accel, Together Fund and Premji Invest. The company described the amount as seed and Series A funding combined and did not disclose a valuation.
A CRM that fills itself from conversations
At the center of Dreamteam is what it calls the Company Brain, a running memory built from customer conversations, emails, meetings and workflows. It pulls out buyer intent, objections, competitor mentions and stakeholder dynamics. The company argues that legacy CRMs, built around structured fields and hand-coded workflows, cannot hold signals like a prospect hesitating on price or a board suddenly scrutinizing costs. It says an account that changes hands carries over the customer’s goals, objections and open commitments.
Four AI teammates work on top of that memory. Rachel is a research assistant that enriches accounts and contacts. Sally, the sales assistant, preps meetings, drafts follow-up emails and manages tasks. Raj is a RevOps partner that monitors the pipeline, flags at-risk deals and improves forecasts. Alex is a CRM administrator that configures the system from plain-language requests. The company says customers do not have to build or train their own agents.
Humans keep control. A person has to approve any outgoing email, teams set pricing rules and approval limits, and users can see where a recommendation came from and correct what the system remembers. Alongside the human interface, Dreamteam offers an API and a Model Context Protocol server so AI agents such as Claude or ChatGPT can reach the CRM. A feature called Magic Apps lets business users build apps and dashboards in natural language.
The company says more than 100 companies in 13 countries use it, and its press release puts the figure at hundreds across AI, online media, healthcare, manufacturing and consulting. Named customers include invideo, Plex and DMS Health. invideo started with a small pilot and expanded to its whole sales team, and Plex’s co-founder and chief product officer called its compatibility with existing AI tools like Claude “a game changer.” Revenue and pricing were not disclosed.
Three former Freshworks executives
The co-founders are former senior executives at Freshworks. CEO Anand Venkatraman leads sales and go-to-market, Ramesh Parthasarathy leads engineering and Senthil Kanthaswamy leads product. The company says they helped scale Freshworks from its early startup days through its IPO and have built AI applications since the GPT-2 era, scaling them to tens of thousands of businesses. When AI reasoning made it possible for software to understand context and carry out work, they decided to rebuild CRM from scratch rather than layer AI onto existing systems. Dreamteam was founded in 2025 and says it is headquartered in Sacramento, California.
Its blog post names Together Fund and Accel as leads, with Premji Invest participating. Together Fund, founded by Freshworks founder Girish Mathrubootham, is Dreamteam’s first institutional investor. Mathrubootham said the cloud wave created a generation of enterprise software leaders 25 years ago and that AI demands software rebuilt from the ground up, with CRM among the largest categories ripe for disruption. Accel partner Shekhar Kirani said each person on a team sees a different version of the customer because no central system holds the information, and that Dreamteam is building that system with AI agents. He said Accel wants to help redefine the $100 billion-plus CRM market. Premji Invest said CRMs must evolve from systems of record into systems of intelligence and action.
Dreamteam says it plans to extend beyond sales into a shared intelligence layer across the customer lifecycle, from acquisition to upsell. It did not say how it will spend the new funding.
Competitors: AI-native CRMs crowd in
Salesforce and HubSpot still dominate the market and are adding their own agent features. Dreamteam’s closest rivals are newer CRMs designed around AI from the start.
Lightfield pivoted from the AI presentation tool Tome and raised a $47 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz. Britain’s Attio raised a $52 million Series B led by GV. Day AI raised a $20 million Series A led by Sequoia in February and made its CRM platform generally available; its founder, Christopher O’Donnell, previously worked at HubSpot. Monaco , started by former Brex chief revenue officer Sam Blond, raised $35 million led by Founders Fund in February. In Europe, Brevo , which combines marketing and sales channels, raised 500 million euros and became a unicorn last December.
Dreamteam pitches two differences. It ships four prebuilt AI teammates covering research, sales, RevOps and admin, so customers do not build agents themselves. And its founders helped grow Freshworks into a public CRM and customer-support software company. But with no valuation, revenue or pricing disclosed, it is hard to tell how this round compares with its rivals’.

candidates.title: Freshworks alums raise $53M to take on Salesforce, HubSpot with AI-native CRM
candidates.snippet: Freshworks alums raise $53M to take on Salesforce, HubSpot with AI-native CRM TechCrunch
candidates.text:
Dreamteam , a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge.
The funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest. The San Francisco-based startup declined to disclose the size of each round or its valuation.
Traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date. That often leaves businesses with incomplete or outdated information. Dreamteam aims to eliminate much of that work by automatically capturing context from sources including emails and customer conversations. It also uses AI agents to handle tasks such as follow-ups, meeting preparation, and pipeline monitoring.
Dreamteam co-founder and CEO Anand Venkatraman (pictured above, right) told TechCrunch that he had repeatedly encountered problems with traditional CRM platforms over more than 25 years in enterprise software, including at Salesforce and Freshworks. Salespeople spent considerable time updating records, yet managers still struggled to get a reliable picture of their business. “In all these years, I have never come across an instance where I could click a button and get a forecast from the CRM,” he said.
That experience led Venkatraman to co-found Dreamteam in 2025 with Senthil Kanthaswamy (pictured above, center), who spent more than nine years at Freshworks, most recently as a product leader at Freshservice, and Ramesh Parthasarathy (pictured above, left), who previously worked on AI and platform engineering at Freshworks.
At the heart of Dreamteam’s CRM is what it calls the Company Brain. This acts as virtual memory, pulling together information from emails, meetings, and other customer interactions to build a shared record of customer relationships. Four built-in AI agents use that information to research prospects, draft follow-up emails, flag potential risks to deals, and configure CRM workflows, with sales teams retaining control over what gets sent to customers.
Dreamteam has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling its product, with most paying for the service, Venkatraman said. The startup has also replaced established CRM platforms at several businesses, including Salesforce at healthcare company DMS Health and HubSpot at other customers.
The advertising sales team at media streaming company Plex also chose Dreamteam over HubSpot and other AI-native CRM alternatives, Venkatraman told TechCrunch. Plex’s co-founder and chief product officer Scott Olechowski said Dreamteam’s ability to integrate with AI tools already used across the company was a “game changer.”
Replacing established CRM platforms at scale may prove more difficult. In a blog post earlier this year, venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) argued that while AI could transform how businesses manage customer relationships, existing CRMs are likely to remain the systems where customer records are stored, with a new generation of AI-powered tools capturing much of the value by working on top of them.
Venkatraman acknowledged that Salesforce and HubSpot are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but noted that their entrenched positions do not guarantee they will dominate the next generation of CRM software.
“We see this as an electric-car moment for systems of record,” he said, adding that AI requires a fundamental rethink of how CRMs are built — not simply adding new features to existing platforms.
Kanthaswamy believes startups have a window of two to five years to gain ground before established CRM providers can fully adapt to AI. Rebuilding software around a fundamentally different architecture takes time, he stated, giving newer companies an opportunity to attract customers while incumbents work to overhaul their existing products.
Dreamteam also plans to expand beyond sales into other parts of the customer lifecycle, including onboarding, customer support, and upselling. The startup already has a feature called Magic Apps that allows users to create custom applications and dashboards within the CRM using natural-language instructions, without writing code.
Currently, Dreamteam employs more than 35 people, with its engineering team based in Chennai and its go-to-market operations in the United States. Kanthaswamy said the startup aims to reach eight figures in annual revenue by the end of 2027, though he declined to disclose the startup’s current revenue.

Arcturus Therapeutics has expanded its collaboration with Meiji Seika Pharma through a $50 million equity investment, an additional technology license and a proposed pandemic preparedness partnership in Japan.
Meiji will purchase unregistered Arcturus securities at $20.27 per share, an 80% premium under the announced transaction terms. Its investment will represent approximately 7.9% of outstanding shares following the transaction.
The companies also signed an exclusive license covering the application of Arcturus’s ARCT-154 technology in an undisclosed therapeutic area.
Separately, a memorandum of understanding establishes principal terms for a potential collaboration and license agreement involving pandemic preparedness and response in Japan. That arrangement remains subject to a definitive agreement.
Arcturus intends to use the investment to support its cystic fibrosis program and accelerate ARCT-2601, an investigational treatment for ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency.
ARCT-2601 is the first mRNA therapeutic intended to use the company’s LUNAR 2.0 delivery platform. Its development is expected to contribute to clinical evaluation of that next-generation technology.
President and CEO Joseph Payne said the expanded relationship reflects Meiji’s confidence in the company’s capabilities and platform.
Founded in 2013 and based in San Diego, Arcturus develops mRNA medicines focused on liver and respiratory diseases.
Its technologies include lipid-mediated delivery and self-amplifying RNA. The company also developed KOSTAIVE, a self-amplifying mRNA COVID vaccine.
Other collaborations include work with Thermo Fisher Scientific, BARDA and Japanese manufacturing joint venture ARCALIS.
Meiji’s investment adds capital while extending an existing strategic relationship across development, licensing and potential public-health applications.
The company’s pipeline programs remain subject to clinical development, regulatory review and other requirements before potential commercialization.

SAN FRANCISCO , Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Numa , the AI Operating System for dealerships, today announced a $45 million Series C led by Blue Cloud Ventures, with participation from Threshold Ventures, Costanoa, Touring Capital, Gradient Ventures and Tokio Marine Future Fund. The round brings Numa's total funding to $96 million. It caps a year in which Numa tripled in size, tripled its annual recurring revenue and became the AI system GM, FordDirect, BMW and Stellantis each put in front of their dealerships.
Numa has already won the hardest part of the dealership: the customer conversation. The system has handled more than 1 billion calls, texts and chats and booked more than 4 million appointments. Dealerships that run on Numa stay and grow with it. Net revenue retention has risen over the past year, and more dealerships are moving to longer agreements.
For decades, dealership software was built one task at a time. Each system kept its own record of what happened, and none of them acted on what the customer just said. The first wave of AI did not change that. It answered faster, then handed the work back to people to chase by hand.
Numa does not hand the work back. It knows not just who the customer is but what they need, and it acts on it: booking the visit, finding the right car, routing the call or flagging the customer about to leave.
"In two years, every general manager will have an AI COO," said Tasso Roumeliotis, founder and CEO of Numa. "At more than 1,500 dealerships, they already do, and it is Numa. It knows every conversation in the store, sees what needs attention and runs the work that follows. That is not another dashboard or another point tool. It is an operating system. TKTMJ Wins $42.4 Million Army Corps Construction Contract In Louisiana
TKTMJ has received a $42.4 million Army contract for construction and site work in Metairie, Louisiana. The Natchitoches, Louisiana-based small business will provide construction access to the work site, demolition, clearing and grubbing, excavation, embankment placement, geotextile and stone installation, and turf establishment and maintenance.
The firm-fixed-price contract was competitively procured through an internet solicitation. The government received four bids.
Work will be performed in Metairie and is expected to be completed by November 15, 2027. The contract is identified as W912P8-27-C-A003.
The full $42.4 million contract amount was obligated when the award was made using fiscal 2027 civil expenses funding.
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers’ New Orleans District is the contracting activity. The district oversees flood-risk management, navigation, coastal restoration, environmental, and other civil works projects throughout southern Louisiana.
Although the announcement does not name the specific project, the listed activities indicate a substantial civil construction effort involving preparation, earthwork, ground reinforcement, stone placement, and final site stabilization.
Construction access work will allow personnel and equipment to reach the active site. Demolition, clearing, and grubbing will remove existing structures, vegetation, debris, and other obstructions before excavation begins.
Excavation and embankment placement will reshape the site in accordance with the project design. Geotextiles can separate, reinforce, filter, or stabilize soil layers, while stone is commonly used for drainage, erosion control, structural support, or surface protection.
Turf establishment and maintenance will stabilize completed areas and restore ground cover after major construction activity.
The firm-fixed-price structure establishes an agreed amount for the defined scope, placing much of the performance-cost risk on TKTMJ unless the government authorizes changes.
Because the Army Corps obligated the entire amount at award, the $42.4 million represents a funded contract rather than an ordering ceiling or value dependent on unexercised options.

The round also included participation from Horizons Ventures, Radical Ventures, Public Sector Pension Investment Board (PSP Investments).
Homebuilders are under increasing pressure to expand housing production, but scaling through traditional construction methods alone is constrained by skilled labor availability and the complexity of adding production capacity market by market. Promise Robotics addresses that constraint by giving builders access to automated production capacity without requiring them to develop and operate factories themselves. The funding round will support the continued expansion of that production network across North America.
This announcement comes just weeks after Promise Robotics expanded its U.S. production network and signed a multi-year commercial agreement with D.R. Horton, America's largest homebuilder by volume. Horton's adoption underscores growing demand for scalable, technology-driven homebuilding solutions. With production already live in Calgary and Nisku, Canada, more than 2,500 housing units under contract across three markets, and its first U.S. facility planned for Phoenix, the company is demonstrating the momentum and operating scale this new investment will help accelerate.
FaaS gives a broad range of homebuilders across geographies access to an integrated production platform that takes existing home designs and translates them into a coordinated production process spanning robotic manufacturing, factory operations, and onsite installation. Through FaaS, builders can access automated production capacity without developing and operating their own factories, helping them improve cycle times, increase capacity, and scale more predictably across communities and markets.

Promise Robotics has taken a measured, capital-efficient approach to growth. Over the past six years, the company has strategically invested in building its proprietary technology platform, validating its business model, and achieving critical operational milestones while steadily expanding its production network into new markets, including its recent entry into Phoenix, AZ.
As housing shortages continue to impact communities across North America, Promise Robotics' automation and AI-driven manufacturing will play a critical role in increasing housing production while improving efficiency, quality and predictability throughout the construction process.

candidates.text:
In a war zone where drones fly in large fleets, human operators cannot supervise every vehicle. When electronic warfare cuts off satellite navigation, each machine has to work out where it is and what surrounds it on its own. The EU aims to mobilise €800 billion in defence spending by 2030 and is planning a European Drone Wall to defend its eastern flank, which makes that kind of autonomy more valuable. A Munich startup working on this spatial awareness problem has raised a Series A.
SE3 combines computer vision and AI to turn sensor data into three-dimensional understanding so machines can decide and move on their own. It is developing the technology for environments where systems must keep working when satellite navigation is disrupted, and its immediate market is European defence.
The product is a spatial intelligence software layer for unmanned systems. It connects drones and ground vehicles from different manufacturers and fuses their sensor data into a shared 3D picture of the environment. It then adjusts behaviour, routes and positions for each vehicle in a swarm, and operators can command all functions by voice. The software runs entirely on the edge, so systems keep operating in contested environments.
SE3 also stresses that it is not tied to any one manufacturer’s vehicles. Modular procurement approaches such as MOSA and Germany’s MOSABw programme are making it easier for armed forces to combine systems from different suppliers, and the company sees growing demand for independent software that works across platforms without competing with the vehicles themselves.
In the past two years, SE3 has shipped thousands of systems, and it is working on multiple contracts with Ukraine and Germany’s armed forces, the Bundeswehr. It is an AI partner to defence primes including Rheinmetall and HENSOLDT and to scale-ups such as Auterion and ERC System. Auterion CEO Lorenz Meier said SE3’s spatial intelligence runs on Auterion’s Skynode, so customers get the capability on platforms they already operate, regardless of manufacturer.
SE3 spun out of the computer vision lab of Professor Daniel Cremers at the Technical University of Munich (TUM). Lukas Köstler is CEO and co-founder, and Simon Klenk is CTO. Both worked on PhDs in computer vision and robotics in that lab. Cremers is chief science officer, holds TUM’s chair for computer vision and AI, and won the Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Prize, Germany’s most prestigious research award.
SE3 announced the $30 million Series A on November 12. Accel led the round, with Keen , Lakestar and Seedcamp participating. Accel partner Matt Robinson said a team with talent from one of Europe’s leading research departments is well placed to build spatial AI for autonomous systems, a problem defence primes have found difficult.
The company will use the funds to grow its engineering, commercial and operations teams and fulfil further contracts. It plans to strengthen its presence in Germany and Ukraine, open a UK office and expand across Europe. Defence remains the focus, with robotics, emergency response and other civilian uses to be explored from 2027.
Capital Keeps Flowing to European Defence Startups
European defence startups have been raising large rounds. Helsing , Europe’s largest defence AI company, raised $1.8 billion in a Series E at an $18 billion valuation. Germany’s Stark, a drone maker, raised a €500 million Series C at a €3.5 billion valuation and won German military contracts worth hundreds of millions of euros within two years of its founding.
TEKEVER , a European maker of autonomous unmanned aircraft, raised a $580 million Series D at a $6.4 billion valuation. France’s Harmattan AI became a unicorn less than two years after its founding with a $200 million Series B. UK counter-drone startup Cambridge Aerospace won a UK Ministry of Defence contract for its low-cost drone interceptor and raised a $300 million Series C at a $3.4 billion valuation.
Many of these companies build the airframes or interceptors themselves, while SE3 builds no vehicles and offers software that runs on systems from several manufacturers. In GPS-denied drone navigation, US-based Theseus, a Y Combinator company, is working on similar ground. In the US, Shield AI raised $2 billion at a $12.7 billion valuation and Anduril raised a $5 billion Series H at a $61 billion valuation.

Tendrils Raises $30 Million To Rebuild General-Purpose Computing
By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 11:17 PM
Tendrils Raises $30 Million To Rebuild General-Purpose Computing
Tendrils has raised $30 million to develop a new processor architecture designed around thousands of parallel computing cores.
Benchmark led the round, with participation from Visionaries Club, the UK Sovereign AI Fund, FR8, Antimatter, Cloudberry VC, Conviction, Embassy Ventures, and SV Angel. Angel investors also participated, and Jack Altman has joined the company’s board.
Tendrils is attempting to redesign the central processing unit without the backward-compatibility constraints associated with conventional sequential and single-core architectures.
The company argues that modern CPUs continue to inherit architectural decisions dating back to the 1970s. In its view, cache-coherency protocols, reorder buffers, shared mutable memory, and linear instruction sequences create complexity that limits efficient scaling.
Rather than modifying existing architectures, Tendrils is building a processor intended to have thousands of cores operating in parallel. That approach requires the company to develop hardware and software together.
Tendrils is therefore working on Vine, an open-source programming language designed from the outset for parallel-first computer architectures. The company believes closer coordination between language design and processor architecture can eliminate legacy requirements and enable more scalable general-purpose computing.
The funding will support the research, engineering, and development required to turn this concept into functioning hardware and software. Tendrils is also recruiting hardware and software engineers interested in developing the architecture.
Although AI accelerators have demonstrated the value of highly parallel computing for specialized workloads, Tendrils is targeting general-purpose applications. The company’s objective is to create an architecture that can support a wider range of software without relying on the sequential design assumptions embedded in conventional processors.

candidates.title: Medical Robotics Startup MedInTech Raises USD 25.7M Series C to Expand AI Robotic Endoscopes Into Surgical Robots
candidates.snippet: Medical Robotics Startup MedInTech Raises USD 25.7M Series C to Expand AI Robotic Endoscopes Into Surgical Robots Wowtale
candidates.text:
MedInTech , a medical robotics startup, has raised a SeriesC round of USD 25.7 million (33.8 billion won). It plans to use the money to broaden its AI robotic endoscope lineup and move from diagnostic endoscopes into higher-value treatment and surgical applications.
Existing investor Atinum Investment and new investor KB Investment co-led the round. Existing investors Smilegate Investment , SL Investment , ICF (Nextrans) and Wooshin Venture Investment joined with follow-on investments. K2 Investment Partners came in as a new investor. The funds were paid in on the 2nd and 13th, and MedInTech plans to close the Series C round with additional funding within the year.
MedInTech previously raised a Series A of USD 6.1 million (8 billion won) in 2022 and a Series B of USD 15.2 million (20 billion won) in 2024. Including the new round, its cumulative funding comes to about USD 47.3 million (62.2 billion won). Since the Series B, the company has been running clinical validation and commercialization of its AI robotic endoscope and building domestic and overseas distribution. The new round provides the funds for a wider product portfolio and next-generation surgical robot development.
Autonomous steering as the core technology
Founded in 2020, MedInTech develops AI robotic endoscopes that combine robotic precision control and artificial intelligence with gastrointestinal endoscopy, a field that has relied on manual operation by clinicians for decades. Its flagship product, INTION S, uses motor-based precision control. In conventional endoscopes, clinicians steer by pulling wires by hand.
The company says its core strength is extending AI from image analysis to controlling the physical movement of a medical device. Existing medical AI has mostly been used to detect lesions in images or support clinical judgment. MedInTech has built autonomous steering technology that turns what the AI recognizes into endoscope movement. This lowers the operating burden on clinicians and can assist with parts of the procedure, such as steering the scope and tracking lesions.
The robot-drive and precision-control technology developed for diagnostic endoscopes can also be applied to therapeutic endoscopes and surgical robots. MedInTech’s growth strategy is to go beyond competing in the existing endoscope market. It aims to combine AI and robotics that support clinicians’ techniques into a medical physical AI platform covering diagnosis, treatment and surgery.
Clinical results and commercialization
In a clinical trial with 178 adults at Seoul National University Hospital, MedInTech confirmed non-inferiority in key maneuverability measures against conventional mechanical endoscopes. The trial also showed reduced physical fatigue and workload for clinicians. The results were published in the international journal Scientific Reports, and the company has since examined the product’s potential clinical use through multicenter trials.
After launching INTION S in Korea, MedInTech has expanded supply to medical institutions under a distribution agreement with DK Healthcare. It has supplied the product to institutions including the National Fire Service Hospital and Ajou University Hospital, and has recorded initial sales in three overseas markets: Thailand, the Philippines and Mongolia. The company has also commercialized INTION DEEPEYE, AI software that supports detection and classification of abnormal areas in gastric and colon endoscopy images, strengthening its combined hardware and software offering.
Investor views
Yunho Jung, a team lead at Atinum Investment, which co-led the round, said that “MedInTech has laid the groundwork for substantial revenue growth by building a domestic and overseas dealer network.” He said he expects the company’s technological competitiveness and growth potential to be well received in a future initial public offering (IPO).
KB Investment praised MedInTech for the world’s first commercialization of an AI robotic endoscope. It said it focused on the company’s potential to grow into a “global medical AI surgical robot company” that “can innovate even the flexible endoscope surgical robot market, based on technology validated in diagnostic endoscopes.”
Use of funds
MedInTech will spend the funds on two main areas. The first is expanding its AI robotic endoscope scope lineup to meet different clinical settings and clinician needs, and strengthening its existing endoscope business. The second is developing and commercializing surgical robots for internal medicine and surgery, built on the robot control technology it has gained from endoscopes.
By product, the company plans to increase R&D spending, including hiring R&D staff and developing prototypes, and to use the funds across the full commercialization process, including domestic and overseas regulatory approvals and building mass-production capacity. In parallel with a USD 17.3 million (22.8 billion won) multi-ministry advanced medical device R&D program it was selected for in April this year, it will refine its autonomous steering technology and develop ultra-small multi-joint treatment instruments. It aims to speed up development of a next-generation surgical robot platform.
“This Series C funding will be an important opportunity to prepare for the next stage of growth, building on the robotic endoscope technology and commercialization results we have accumulated,” said Chiwon Lee, CEO of MedInTech. “We will expand domestic and overseas supply of our AI robotic endoscope and advance our autonomous steering and precision control technologies to build a next-generation medical robotics platform that extends from diagnosis to treatment and surgery.”

Hardwick Tactical has received a fixed-price, indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract with a maximum value of approximately $20.2 million to produce flame-resistant intermediate-weather jackets for the Air Force.
The Mayaguez, Puerto Rico-based small business will manufacture intermediate weather outer-layer jackets in sage and operational camouflage pattern configurations.

The procurement was competitive, with one response received. The Defense Logistics Agency reported the acquisition as competitive despite receiving a single offer.

Accordingly, the approximately $20.2 million represents the contract’s maximum ordering ceiling rather than guaranteed revenue to Hardwick Tactical. Actual payments will depend on the quantities DLA orders during the five-year period.
The Air Force is the military customer identified for the garments. Intermediate-weather outer layers provide protection in cooler or changing conditions while allowing service members to perform operational duties.
The flame-resistant requirement is particularly important for personnel working near aircraft, fuel, machinery, or other environments where exposure to fire or thermal hazards may occur.
Offering the garment in sage and operational camouflage pattern versions allows DLA to support different uniform and mission requirements.
DLA Troop Support in Philadelphia is the contracting activity for contract SPE1C1-27-D-0014. The organization manages military clothing and textile supply chains, including the procurement of uniforms, protective apparel, and related materials.
The IDIQ structure gives the agency flexibility to place orders based on inventory levels, deployment requirements, sizing demand, and other operational needs.
The award adds a long-term Air Force apparel contract to Hardwick Tactical’s production portfolio while preserving its federal designation as a small business.

Alecto raises $20M seed funding to make UK property law more accessible to consumers with AI
by Kyt Dotson
Alecto Conveyancing Ltd. , a London-based artificial intelligence-native law firm, today announced it raised $20 million in seed funding led by Insight Partners to make the law more accessible to the general public.
Firstminute Capital, Blue Lion Global, Andrena Ventures, FJ Labs, Antiportfolio Ventures, the Rigby Group and Mischon de Reya LLP also joined in the round. Angel investors participating in the round included Octopus Group Chief Executive and founder Simon Rogerson and SwiftKey founder John Reynolds.
Founded in September 2025 by CEO Will Rice (pictured), a serial entrepreneur who previously built fintech mortgage lender Gen H, Alecto’s first service targets the United Kingdom conveyancing market, the legal work required to buy and sell property. Rice drew on his experience building a mortgage company and decided to focus initially on bringing more people into ownership. With that expertise, Alecto aims to use AI to help give everyday people greater access to the law.
Alecto argues that traditional legal services are starved, with too few qualified attorneys and too few hours a day. Billing is based on hours, not outcomes and the service model doesn’t lean toward customers; this leads to unpredictable costs and a process that leaves customers in the dark.
The law firm said it’s using AI and legal experts to explain opaque legal processes in plain language and help clients make informed decisions. The company intends to target the property conveyancing market, which represents almost $3.3 billion in the U.K. alone, and aims to become the number one leader in property legal services by 2027.
“For too long, the legal industry has expected customers to work on its terms; now, AI presents the opportunity to put the consumer in control,” Rice said. “People don’t want to buy a lawyer’s time; they want results. Alecto exists to make the law accessible to everyone, giving control back to the consumer.”
Consumer legal services in the U.K. value growth pushed revenue over £55 billion, around $72.5 billion, in 2026, according to a report from Research and Markets . Business and commercial practices lead with 51% market value, followed by growth in the injury and conveyancing law markets.
“Property is where we prove the model. We’re building the technology and operations to rapidly break into new countries and new areas of law,” Rice added. “Ultimately, access to exceptional legal support should not depend on how much money you have or how confidently you can navigate the system.”

Danish biotech specialist raises €20 million to accelerate market-ready trait development

Danish biotechnology company Traitomic has raised €20 million in a Series A round led by Sofinnova Partners. The investor consortium also includes the Export and Investment Fund of Denmark (EIFO), Footprint Firm, Nordic Foodtech VC, PSV Hafnium and SVG Ventures. The round marks Traitomic's first external investment since its spin-out from Carlsberg and follows the development of a growing customer base across multiple industries. The funding will support international expansion and continued development of the company's scientific and commercial capabilities.
The world increasingly depends on improved biological performance to address challenges in food security, resource efficiency and sustainability. Yet translating a biological need into a commercially relevant trait can be slow, fragmented and difficult to scale. Traitomic helps bridge that gap not only by developing market-ready traits, but also supporting customers from initial commercial challenges through to deployment.
© Traitomic (L-R) Toni Wendt, Technology Lead; Jan Gottlieb, Commercial Lead; Gustav Hambraeus, Managing Director
Traitomic's proprietary FIND-IT platform identifies specific genetic variants in conventionally bred populations without gene editing, enabling rapid trait development while maintaining broad regulatory and commercial applicability. Unlike many trait-development approaches that are tailored to specific organism types, the platform can be applied across both plant and microbial systems.
To date, Traitomic has delivered 116 traits to 47 customers across 32 organisms spanning plant breeding and seed; food supply chain and precision nutrition; and biosolutions and industrial biotech. The projects range from improving crop robustness and yield, to developing differentiated food products with enhanced flavour, nutrition or shelf life, and optimising enzymes and strains used in industrial biotechnology. This breadth of applications reflects demand from customers across multiple industries and highlights the significant opportunity to expand trait development across the broader bioeconomy.

The funding will support Traitomic's international expansion and help the company capture this opportunity across food, agriculture and biosolutions markets. In addition, Traitomic will continue to broaden its integrated offering, enabling closer collaboration with customers from initial biological or commercial challenges through delivery of market-ready traits.
Gustav Hambraeus, CEO and co-founder, Traitomic said: "This investment marks the beginning of Traitomic's next chapter. Over the past years, we have demonstrated that customers across the food value chain are looking for faster routes from biological insight to commercial impact. With the support of our new investors, we can now expand internationally, deepen our collaboration with customers and bring our integrated approach to trait development to many more innovation challenges."
© Traitomic
Michael Krel, Partner, Sofinnova Partners said: "Traitomic has demonstrated something that is rare in biological innovation: the ability to develop commercially relevant traits across a broad range of organisms and applications. Combined with the company's strong customer traction and proven track record, this creates a compelling foundation for future growth. We believe Traitomic is well positioned to become a leading partner for trait development across agriculture, food and industrial biotechnology, and we look forward to supporting the team with both capital and experience as they enter their next phase of international expansion."
Anders Røed, Executive Vice President, Group Strategy and Commercial, Carlsberg said: "Traitomic is an excellent example of how fundamental research can create value far beyond its original field of application. FIND-IT was developed at Carlsberg Research Laboratory to improve barley, and it is now enabling advances in agriculture, food production and industrial biotechnology. I am proud of what the team has achieved and excited to continue supporting the company as it enters this next phase of international growth."

SAN FRANCISCO , Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Following its $20 million Series A at a $202 million valuation and fivefold revenue growth in six months, WhiteMatter , formerly QuilrAI, today announced two senior hires to accelerate its global expansion. Jasmine Wu, formerly senior marketing executive of Proofpoint and ByteDance, the parent company of TikTok, joins WhiteMatter as Chief Marketing Officer, while Anuj Gupta, former Managing Director of Hitachi Systems India, joins as Managing Director, Asia Pacific & Japan (APJ). They join Chief Revenue Officer Tammy Sexton, who joined in late 2025, as WhiteMatter builds out its leadership team to meet growing global demand for AI agent governance.
Continue Reading
Jasmine Wu joins as Chief Marketing Officer and Anuj Gupta as Managing Director, Asia Pacific & Japan
WhiteMatter was founded by CEO Vidit Arora, a founding member of Securonix who spent more than a decade helping build the security analytics company, leading across product, solution architecture, and global customer experience. He created WhiteMatter to solve a new security challenge: how companies govern AI agents that can make decisions, access systems, and take action on their own. WhiteMatter helps enterprises assess and approve agents before they go live, then continuously control what they can access and do in production. The company has received acquisition offers but is instead focusing on building and scaling the business independently. The new appointments bring the marketing, sales, and leadership needed to support that growth.
"When AI began moving from a tool people use to agents that make autonomous decisions, I watched the traditional security model start to break," said Arora. "I founded WhiteMatter on the belief that companies would need to rethink security and infrastructure for a world built around AI and agents. That world is here. Enterprises are scaling agents now, and they need governance based on how agents actually behave, starting from pre-production blueprints. Jasmine, Anuj, and Tammy have each built and scaled category-defining businesses, and they give us the go-to-market strength to deliver that governance worldwide."
Wu joins from Proofpoint, where she served as Head of Product Marketing and GTM Operations as the company grew from under $1 billion to more than $2 billion in annual recurring revenue. Before that, she was Head of Marketing at ByteDance, the parent company of TikTok. Her career spans 15+ years across security and consumer technology at global scale. At WhiteMatter, she will lead global marketing to establish WhiteMatter as the company defining the agent and AI lifecycle governance category.
"The AI and agent challenge extends far beyond security, yet it has been treated as a security problem for too long," said Wu. "Enterprises are deploying thousands of agents and AI workflows powered by non-deterministic models, but runtime protection alone cannot govern an agent that was never properly assessed before deployment. We believe AI and agent governance must be approached as a lifecycle: from the moment an agent is proposed to every execution in production, with a complete record of the decisions made along the way. This requires a fundamentally different approach, and a company built specifically to deliver it. That company is WhiteMatter. Grey matter is where agents think and act; white matter connects and protects them. We are building that critical layer for the agentic enterprise."
Anuj Gupta's appointment marks WhiteMatter's entry into Asia Pacific and Japan, one of the fastest-moving markets for enterprise AI adoption. He joins from Hitachi Systems India, where as Managing Director and CEO, he helped grow a $10.6 million business into a $425 million industry leader. He was also instrumental in the successful integration of Micro Clinic and its transition into the Hitachi Systems global network, contributing significantly to the organization's growth, operational evolution, and expanded market presence. At WhiteMatter, he will lead APJ market entry and expansion, building a regional ecosystem of partners, enterprise customers, and technology alliances.
"Asia Pacific and Japan represent a significant opportunity for enterprise AI, but adoption has to move hand in hand with governance and accountability," said Gupta. "Enterprises here are deploying agents at the same pace as the US, often with leaner security teams and stricter regulators. A deployment-first approach lets them govern an agent once, before it goes live, instead of chasing every action after. That is how we help organizations embrace AI with confidence, and that is the model we are bringing to APJ."
The two hires join Sexton, who leads WhiteMatter's revenue strategy. She has years of experience selling security at LaunchDarkly, Skyflow, and Sumo Logic, with a track record of scaling sales teams through hypergrowth at venture-backed technology companies.

BOSTON , Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ODAIA , an AI company delivering predictive commercial intelligence for pharma, today announced it has closed a US$15 million Series C financing led by Monograph Capital and anchored by strategic investor PHM , the leading health media agency in the U.S., part of Publicis Groupe. Investors from ODAIA's earlier rounds are also returning: BDC Capital , Flint Capital , Innospark Ventures , and Graphite Ventures from its Series A and Threshold Ventures and Wittington Ventures from its Series B. ODAIA will use the capital to grow within the enterprise pharma accounts it already serves and continue innovating its commercial intelligence platform.
Leading biopharmaceutical companies use ODAIA for commercial intelligence and workflow automations for field and marketing teams across many therapeutic areas. ODAIA predicts patient journeys, uncovers missed Rx opportunities, determines which healthcare professionals (HCPs) to prioritize through which channels, and keeps sales and marketing working from one brand strategy.
"Pharma has proven that AI works in commercial. The hard part now is scaling it," said Philip Poulidis , CEO and co-founder of ODAIA. "Most companies can show results on one brand, and every new brand or therapeutic area still costs another team and another build. ODAIA started by helping field teams decide where to focus. Today our platform is the commercial intelligence infrastructure that scales what's working across brand, marketing, and field teams, and across a company's whole portfolio. This round lets us go deeper with the enterprise customers we already serve and, with PHM, bring that infrastructure to more of the industry, faster."
"We have watched the ODAIA team turn predictive AI into decisions that pharma brand and field teams act on every day," said Charles Conn , co-founder and partner at Monograph Capital, which co-led ODAIA's Series B and led this round. "The ODAIA team has a track record of helping large and specialty pharma brands reach the physicians whose patients need their therapies most."
One strategy for brand, field, and marketing
Inside most pharma companies, data sits in many systems owned by separate teams, so brand, marketing, and field each work from a different picture of the same physician. Patients get missed, field and digital effort lands in the wrong places, and nobody can say with confidence what is influencing HCP decisions. ODAIA's commercial intelligence platform provides the foundation underneath. It brings disparate data, field sales activity, and digital engagement into one view of each HCP that brand, marketing, and field teams all work from.
Brand teams codify their strategy once in Brand Strategy Studio , and ODAIA's decision engines turn it into HCP-level choices about who to reach, through which channel, when, and with what message. Extending to a new brand or therapeutic area is a matter of configuration. The platform identifies physicians whose patients are likely to need a therapy, often months before a diagnosis shows up in the data. Field Intelligence delivers prioritized call plans to field teams inside their CRM, and Marketing Intelligence orchestrates individualized HCP journeys across digital and partner channels.
Every ODAIA recommendation comes with the reasoning behind it, so commercial and compliance teams can see why. Commercial leaders ask questions of their data in plain language and get finished analysis in minutes. The platform continuously measures engagement and prescription lift and feeds the results into the next decision, so teams can adjust as markets change.
Alongside the financing, ODAIA signed a commercial Platform Agreement that makes PHM, Publicis Groupe's U.S. health media agency, ODAIA's exclusive agency partner in the U.S.
ODAIA continues to work directly with pharma companies, and its platform works alongside the CRM, in-house analytics models, and data infrastructure each brand already uses. The partnership connects signals across digital media and field sales so clients can coordinate HCP engagement across both.
Founded out of the University of Toronto in 2018, ODAIA is headquartered in Toronto with an office in Boston. To learn more about ODAIA's commercial intelligence platform, visit odaia.ai .
About ODAIA
ODAIA is the leading AI company delivering predictive commercial intelligence for pharma. Leading biopharmaceutical companies, from top-20 global organizations to specialty innovators, use ODAIA to uncover missed Rx opportunities, determine which HCPs to prioritize through which channels, and coordinate true omnichannel execution across sales and marketing. By continuously turning HCP and patient signals into real-time actions, ODAIA enables commercial teams to adapt strategy as markets change and activate updated guidance directly within the systems they already use. Learn more at odaia.ai .

Key facts
Hatz AI raised $24 million in Series A funding.
Josh Schertzer of Nadia Partners led the deal.

Source: Hatz AI
NEW YORK, UNITED STATES — Hatz AI, which sells its artificial intelligence (AI) platform to small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) only through managed service providers (MSPs), has raised $24 million in Series A funding. Nadia Partners, Vestigo Ventures and The Private Shares Fund backed the round.
Josh Schertzer, a partner at Nadia Partners and former chief technology officer at Blackstone, led the deal.
AI sold under the MSP’s brand
Hatz announced the funding in a press release on Nov. 12.
Its platform gives MSPs multi-tenant AI governance, custom workflows and automated routing across leading foundation models. MSPs can then package and deliver AI-as-a-Service under their own brand.
Hatz said it has no competing direct-to-enterprise sales and has issued more than 15,000 AI certifications to builders globally.
The investment will help it scale a partner network that it said spans thousands of MSPs in all 50 U.S. states, nine Canadian provinces and nine countries.
Partners triple, staff quadruple
Hatz said its active MSP partner count tripled year over year, while revenue grew even faster. It expanded its workforce from 14 to nearly 60 employees.
The company is expanding in Flatiron, New York City, and scaling its forward deployed engineer team to work alongside partners. It is also growing its AI research and AI optimization teams.
“Small businesses represent the backbone of the global economy, and the managed service providers they already rely on are exactly the people to lead this transformation,” said Jimmy Hatzell, chief executive and co-founder of Hatz AI.
“By giving MSPs full control over governance, spend, and deployment, we’re making it possible for every small business to become AI native,” Hatzell said.
What the money funds
The new capital will deepen platform capabilities, including Hatz’s auto-model routing engine, benchmarks and internal software factory infrastructure. Hatz will also keep recruiting engineers for its forward deployed engineering and AI research units.
“By focusing exclusively on powering MSPs rather than trying to sell directly to end-users, Hatz has built a true dominance in channel-delivered AI,” Schertzer said.
What it means for buyers
Investors are backing a model in which smaller companies get AI from the IT provider they already pay, rather than from the model makers directly. For businesses that buy managed services or information technology outsourcing (ITO) , that puts AI governance and spending decisions into an existing contract.
